title: Rethinking Human Intent-to-CAD: Parametric CAD Model Generation via Cooperative Multi-Task Alignment and Spatial-Aware Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Parametric Computer-Aided-Design (CAD) modeling from human intent remains challenging, particularly during the conceptual design stage, where design goals are expressed through incomplete and unstructured modalities (e.g., hand-drawn sketches and textual descriptions). In this work, we rethink the human intent-to-CAD pipeline and propose a unified method that directly maps multi-level human intents to executable codes, without assuming the prior existence of target CAD models. To support our study, we construct HiCAD, the first large-scale dataset aligning hand-drawn sketches, textual descriptions, and parametric CAD codes. Based on this, we introduce HiCAD, a two-stage framework comprising Cooperative Multi-Task Alignment to bridge the representational gap between heterogeneous inputs, and Spatial-Aware Reinforcement Learning to enforce geometric and topological consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing baselines across multiple tasks, validating its effectiveness and robustness in transforming heterogeneous human intents into high-fidelity parametric CAD models. Our project page: https://zqwlearning.github.io/HiCAD.

title: See Me, Believe Me: Causality, Intersectionality, and Interventions Improving the Appearance of Patients
abstract: In the context of medical records, patients often experience testimonial injustice, where the textual account undermines the validity of their experiences. Past work has demonstrated that intersectionality of demographic features is crucial to detect such injustice. We use causal discovery to study the degree to which certain demographic features tied to marginalization (namely age, gender, and race), together lead to specific types of testimonial injustice terms. This offers us an insightful Structural Causal Model (SCM) relating those demographic features to the different ways a patients' reality may be undermined. We then move toward addressing such injustice, by very selectively (based on insights from the SCM) editing physicians' notes. For comparison, we contrast these rule-based edits with blanket context-based modifications using an LLM. We assess the impact of these changes on the perception of patients' experiences, using human experts and an LLM. We find that edits, in general, enhance clarity regarding the urgency and causes of patients' conditions. Additionally, for human experts, rule-based modifications show a tendency to shift blame away from patients, and toward more objective external factors. These findings (1) underscore the importance of quantifying sources of injustice in how patients' testimonies are recorded, (2) reveal that making minimal intentional changes accordingly can effect improved patient perception, and (3) call for larger efforts to assess health outcomes under such more just representation.

title: Kernel-only Lean proof that the rank of 3×3 matrix multiplication over F2 is 23
abstract: The Lean 4 proof, checked entirely by the Lean kernel, that the tensor rank of 3×3 matrix multiplication over F2 is 23, for the paper The rank of 3×3 matrix multiplication over F2 is 23 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23304897, arXiv:2610.11823). The final theorem R22K.Final.rank_ge_23 depends only on the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. This is release v1.0 of github.com/tejasvi/rank333-f2-kernel, commit 0c7c6173c3dc91cf63972f1fe8980b726dd6a8e6. Its README describes the contents: SHA256SUMS gives the SHA-256 hash of every file, VERIFICATION.md the checks, and REGENERATE.md how every package is regenerated from the inputs with the programs in generators/. The private parts of the modules were deleted after they were built and checked, so a full replay regenerates them. The repository at v1.0 is in this record as rank333-f2-kernel-v1.0.zip. The other files of this record are listed, with their sizes, SHA-256 hashes and contents, in the repository's ZENODO.md.

title: The Proof Already Contains the Program: One rewrite theory from every logic to running code
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: Trust in a proof is supposed to rest on a kernel small enough to read by hand. The formal-methods ecosystem has instead grown a dozen large, mutually opaque kernels—one per proof assistant—and now machine learning floods all of them with proofs and programs no human can eyeball. We report a working demonstration that the escape from this predicament is a single, small, well-understood mathematical object: the λΠ-calculus modulo rewriting, a typed lambda calculus with user computation rules into which functional type theories are known to embed. We realize eight source systems—Coq/CIC, Lean 4, HOL Light, Isabelle/Pure, Agda, Metamath, GHC's System FC, and Rust's typed MIR—as exact, faithfully translated images inside one such checker, so that eight trust roots collapse to one. Then we show the same object runs in reverse: because a constructive proof already contains its program (the Brouwer–Heyting–Kolmogorov reading of Curry–Howard), the checked content of each image extracts, through one back-end, to a whole-program Rust artifact that a compiler builds and runs against a certified differential—for all eight languages. One small kernel receives every logic and emits its program. The consequence is a concrete first step toward software engineering done mathematics-first: you audit a tiny shared checker rather than trusting the author, human or machine, and the verified proof is the deployable artifact. A fresh finite logical-entropy estimator now tests that extraction thesis on an object not used to build the original eight-door demonstration: its exact ensemble law is proved in Lean, its Rust realization returns the same unreduced rational pair, and applicable structural mutations are killed. A successor program, reported in §6, has since walked this paper's own roadmap: export depth past scalars, an independent dual-metal differential through the Boundary reducer, an exactly enumerated residual trust base, and a proved composition theorem making source-kernel-to-bare-metal a single certified arrow. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: Three Errors, Not One: The Quantum MacWilliams Identity, Certified
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: A classical bit fails one way: it flips. A qubit fails three ways—X, Z, or both at once—and that single change of arithmetic, from one error per site to three, is the whole difference between the classical theory of error-correcting codes and the quantum one. It has a precise home. The MacWilliams identity of 1963 is the exact law relating a linear code's weight distribution to its dual's; its quantum analogue, due to Shor and Laflamme, carries the same law across the stabilizer formalism with one coefficient changed—a +1 becomes a +3. We prove that quantum identity in the kernel of a proof assistant, and we prove it the honest way: by reusing, unchanged, the finite character-orthogonality argument that certifies the classical identity, isolating the +3 to a single new lemma about the four Pauli operators at one qubit. The classical coefficient is not merely inapplicable to quantum codes; we exhibit a code on which the +1 law is false and its failure is itself a theorem. From the certified identity the entire Shor–Laflamme weight spectrum of a code follows—the count of stabilizers and of logical operators at every weight—and from the spectrum two numbers the field cares about: the code distance (the minimum weight of a logical operator, recovered as the first place the spectra part) and the sub-threshold error-rate prefactor (the count of minimum-weight logical representatives, which the distance alone cannot see). We certify both for the five-qubit perfect code and the Steane code, exhibit the exact spectra, and place the result beside a companion certificate that reaches the distance by a single witness: the witness is a local probe, the enumerator a global census, and a code is fully accounted for only when both have spoken. A public instrument reproduces every number by independent enumeration, trusting neither our kernel nor our word. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: Routing signals for silent-error detection in text-to-SQL over a university data warehouse: benchmark, labels and code
abstract: Supporting data and code for the paper "Does the Router Know? Mixture-of-Experts Routing Signals for Detecting Silent Errors in Text-to-SQL over University Data Warehouses" (submitted to Knowledge-Based Systems, Elsevier). An agentic assistant built on the open-weight Mixture-of-Experts model gpt-oss-120b answers questions in Italian over the live data warehouse of a public university, on premises and without a GPU. Its most damaging failures are silent: a query that runs, returns a plausible number, and answers a different question from the one asked. This deposit contains: a benchmark of 1000 Italian questions from 51 templates, with reference values verified against the institution's own reports and the date each value was read; the error labels for three system configurations, together with the human review behind them and the stratified sample used to validate the references; the assistant's answers as returned; per-layer router statistics for all 36 layers of the model, extracted post hoc by replaying each answer through a teacher-forced forward pass in llama.cpp and capturing the router tensors, validated against the experts the model actually selected; the reports produced by the probes, including AUROC by feature family, control tasks and risk-coverage curves; the semantic layer, that is the official measure behind each institutional report and the catalogue of the 283 warehouse tables; and all the code, from routing extraction to probe evaluation. All material is aggregated. No person-level data was processed or released at any stage. The internal page and API addresses of the institutional dashboard have been removed from two files, which keep the measure definitions and default filters relied on by the paper. Data, labels and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0; the code is additionally available under the MIT licence. Access to the files is currently restricted and granted on request; it will be opened on publication of the article.

title: Timed Reachability in Logic
abstract: Abstract We discuss some recent approaches to game-theoretic semantics (GTS), a useful alternative to the traditional Tarski-style compositional semantics of logic. One attractive feature of GTS is that model-checking upper bounds for logical systems can often be obtained directly by considering the corresponding alternating Turing machines. Our focus is on semantic games equipped with clocks, i.e., resources that control recursive behaviour during play and give rise to timed variants of reachability games. Such clock-based semantic frameworks naturally suggest variants of logical systems with different computational properties. We review some developments related to these themes, focusing on systems derived from the modal $$\mu $$ μ -calculus while also discussing applications to temporal logic.

title: To Use or Not: Differentiating Artificial Intelligence Content for Different Industries
abstract: Artificial Intelligence continues to develop; its integration has rapidly progressed into numerous business industries, impacting business operations regardless of context. This study examines how consumers respond to AI implementation across industries that vary in perceived creativity. Using a survey and a 2 by 2 between- subjects experimental design, this research finds that AI implementation negatively affects consumers’ willingness to purchase, regardless of the perceived creativity level of the industry. Additionally, drawing on research linking gender to differential perceptions of technology, this research shows that the negative effect of AI implementation is stronger for women than for men. Based on the findings, practical implications are offered while limitations are also discussed.

title: Celeus engine validation report
abstract: Validation report for the Celeus statistics engine, generated from a pinned R environment. It lists 111 cases across 39 test types and 281 numeric comparisons. Every case is compared with an independent computation in base R or standard packages; 12 cases are also anchored to a published literature value and 11 carry a certified reference value; 88 are canonical-only and labelled as such. For test selection, the correct test family was proposed in 85 of 93 evaluated cases; 18 of the 111 cases skipped that evaluation because their dataset is fetched externally. Reproducibility is checked separately over a 41-case corpus. This report is not a substitute for review by an independent statistician, and it is research statistics, not clinical decision support.

Every case is compared with an independent computation in base R or standard packages; 12 cases are also anchored to a published literature value and 11 carry a certified reference value; 88 are canonical-only and labelled as such. For test selection, the correct test family was proposed in 85 of 93 evaluated cases; 18 of the 111 cases skipped that evaluation because their dataset is fetched externally. Reproducibility is checked separately over a 41-case corpus. This report is not a substitute for review by an independent statistician, and it is research statistics, not clinical decision support.

title: Systematic Inference Audit and Runtime Telemetry of Aleph Alpha Kolibri-1: Serving Forensics, Token Economics, and Parser Remediation on NVIDIA H200 SXM
abstract: Systematic Inference Audit and Runtime Telemetry of Aleph Alpha Kolibri-1: Serving Forensics, Token Economics, and Parser Remediation on NVIDIA H200 SXM Available in English and German. Both technical reports (PDF), Markdown sources, raw JSONL telemetry, and replication scripts are included in this record. Abstract (English) We present an independent, systematic inference audit of Aleph Alpha's Kolibri-1 model deployed under vLLM on a single NVIDIA H200 SXM (141 GB HBM3e). Comprising 5,372 live requests across four benchmark stages (Probe, Ablation, Stress/Concurrency, and Needle-in-a-Haystack), this audit resolves a critical failure class in LLM production pipelines: the silent failure of naive JSON parsers on reasoning models. Key Empirical Findings: Parser Remediation & Semantic Compliance: An initial 0.0% usable response rate in standard toolchains was isolated as a harness parsing artifact caused by unhandled delimiters. Upon delimiter-aware extraction and Pydantic validation, Kolibri-1 achieved a 99.98% semantic accuracy (5,371 / 5,372 requests correct; 95% Wilson CI lower bound: 99.89%). Token Economics & Fast-Lane Architecture: For routine information extraction, disabling reasoning (enable_thinking: false) reduces generated tokens by ~90% (median 492 to 50 tokens), cutting compute resource allocation by 71% and increasing request throughput by 3.4x on 4k-token unique prompts (up to 8.8x with cached prefixes). Hardware Saturation & The Latency Wall: Prefill compute saturates at ~35,100 prompt tokens/s. Under high concurrency (C=64, 31k context), P95 TTFT is 38.88 s across the full cell due to the synchronized start-burst prefill queue (steady-state P95: 5.0 s). Peak KV-cache utilization reached 42.66% with zero preemptions, demonstrating that H200 capacity is prefill-compute bound rather than memory bound. Enterprise On-Premises Dimensioning: Sizing extrapolations indicate that typical enterprise and legal workloads (e.g., 500 documents/day) utilize < 1% of an H200's prefill capacity. Dual 48 GB PCIe setups (e.g., 2x NVIDIA L40S or RTX 6000 Ada) paired with an intelligent API gateway (Fast Lane vs. Deep Lane) provide a cost-effective on-premises alternative. Kurzfassung (Deutsch) Dieser technische Bericht dokumentiert ein unabhängiges Inferenz-Audit von Aleph Alphas Kolibri-1 auf NVIDIA H200 SXM unter vLLM über 5.372 Live-Requests. Das Audit beweist, dass frühere 0,0-%-Ausfälle in Standard-Toolchains auf unmaskierte Reasoning-Delimiter ( ) im Test-Harness zurückzuführen sind. Nach Implementierung eines strikten Delimiter-Parsings liefert Kolibri-1 eine inhaltliche Genauigkeit von 99,98 %. Durch die Entkopplung von Routine-Extraktion („Fast Lane", Reasoning aus, 50 Tokens) gegenüber komplexer Urteilsfindung („Deep Lane", Reasoning an, 492 Tokens) lässt sich der Durchsatz um das 3,4- bis 8,8-Fache steigern und der Rechenaufwand pro Request um 71 % senken. title: A Lightweight Optimized CNN Framework for Breast Cancer Screening and Subtype Classification
abstract: Breast cancer remains one of the most serious diseases threatening human health globally. To address diagnostic subjectivity and insufficient classification granularity in pathological screening, this study proposes a lightweight complementary convolutional neural network (CNN) framework for two distinct yet clinically related tasks. The first model performs binary classification of invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) (IDC-positive vs. IDC-negative), while the second model conducts fine-grained multiclass classification of four malignant subtypes. Notably, primary patch-level evaluation for the IDC binary task may produce optimistically biased performance due to data leakage, where patches from the same patient can appear in both the training and test sets. The IDC_regular_ps50_idx5 dataset embeds patient/case identifiers within patch filenames, enabling patient-disjoint partitioning to mitigate this risk. On public patch-level test data, the framework achieves a patch-level accuracy of 0.8732 and an AUC of 0.9245, demonstrating superior resource efficiency compared with several state-of-the-art models. Computational analysis shows that the proposed model has 0.435 M parameters and 0.145 G FLOPs—33.8× fewer parameters than VGG16 (convolutional-only), 54.0× fewer than ResNet50, and 9.3× fewer than EfficientNet-B0. To quantify the optimistic bias introduced by patch-level evaluation, we first performed supplementary patient-disjoint 5-fold GroupKFold cross-validation on the IDC dataset using filename-embedded patient identifiers. Under this intra-dataset patient-disjoint protocol, it achieves a mean accuracy of 0.8005 and mean AUC of 0.8783, with a moderate performance drop of approximately 7 percentage points relative to patch-level results. We further conducted external cross-dataset validation on BreakHis with strict patient-disjoint 5-fold GroupKFold cross-validation. Under this cross-dataset protocol, the model yields substantially degraded performance (mean accuracy of 0.5417 ± 0.1738 and mean AUC of 0.5930 ± 0.1680), illustrating significant performance drop when generalizing to completely unseen patients under domain shift. A systematic loss function comparison experiment under patch-level configuration demonstrates that Focal Loss (γ = 2.0) achieves the highest overall patch-level performance (Accuracy = 0.8125, AUC = 0.8980) on the binary IDC identification task, outperforming the baseline cross-entropy loss. The results indicate that the proposed complementary framework achieves competitive classification accuracy with a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off within the IDC dataset; however, strong cross-dataset generalization cannot be guaranteed, and patient-disjoint evaluation on multi-institution matched cohorts is required for real-world clinical deployment. Limitations in generalization to minority classes remain. Future work will focus on constructing multi-institution patient-annotated histopathology cohorts for patient-disjoint evaluation and domain-adaptation techniques to mitigate cross-dataset domain shift.

title: "R2D2-Guard Experimental Records and Reproduction Data"
abstract: "This dataset accompanies the study \u201cR2D2-Guard: Auditable Release Policies for LoRA-Adapted LLM Services.\u201d It contains frozen experimental records for examining how release policies retain, replace, or withhold model responses under clean and backdoor attack conditions. The records cover mathematical reasoning experiments using GSM8K and SVAMP, together with scientific claim verification experiments using SciFact.The materials include request-level model outputs, recorded policy decisions, evaluation annotations, aggregate results, frozen protocols, configuration metadata, figure source data, and audit reports. JSON, JSONL, and CSV files preserve the recorded evidence. Accompanying documentation explains field definitions, provenance, evaluation denominators, and reproduction procedures. The materials support CPU reconstruction of reported tables and inspection of the relationships between requests, policy decisions, and recorded delivery outcomes.Verification software and reproduction instructions are available in the associated R2D2-Guard GitHub repository. Some historical model weights and training inputs are unavailable; the documented limitations distinguish reconstruction of saved results from regeneration of experiments. Reused benchmark components retain their upstream attribution and licensing conditions."

title: Unsupervised Cross-device Speaker Diarization And Linking Through Spatiotemporal Structure
abstract: Linking speakers across independently recorded rooms is difficult because microphone, room, and codec mismatch distort speaker embeddings. We study visitor linking without visitor enrollment or identity labels in simulated outpatient workflows. The proposed method combines per-device embedding centering, concurrency constraints, room-type-specific visit constraints, and a clustering threshold calibrated from concurrent visitors and identified staff voices. On simulated days built from VOiCES recordings, with companions, return visits, walk-ins, silent visits, and acoustic leakage, it improves B$^3$-F1 over the best label-free baseline for all 11 extractors, by 5.3-14.6 points (all 95\% intervals exclude zero). ECAPA-TDNN reaches 86.6, compared with 76.4 for the best label-free baseline and 87.7 for the best oracle-informed baseline. Gains persist across the reported workflow perturbations, but depend on removing duplicated cross-room speech: without this step, the method wins for only 2 of 11 extractors. Single-visit patients also remain vulnerable to false merges. These results support structure-aware linking while identifying preprocessing and identity-safety limitations that must be addressed before clinical deployment.

title: Error-Based Bidirectional Predictive Coding Enables Deep, 4-Bit Predictive Coding Networks
abstract: Predictive coding networks (PCNs) promise properties not offered by backpropagation-trained networks: learning from purely local information, a single network that both discriminates and generates, and flexible inference by energy minimization. However, their iterative inference is expensive, making hardware acceleration desirable, and a useful, efficient accelerator needs both depth and aggressive quantization. Canonical state-based PC delivers neither: its inference signal decays exponentially with depth, so deep models fail to train, and low precision makes it worse. We show that pairing two recent methods carries the full PCN property set into the deep, 4-bit regime: bidirectional PC (bPC), which unifies discrimination and generation, and the error-based reparameterization (ePC), which optimizes prediction errors rather than states during inference. Error optimization delivers the output signal to every layer in a single backward pass, removing the signal decay; one additional element, global-norm clipping of the error gradients, stabilizes the error dynamics at depth. The resulting ePC+bPC model trains stably up to at least eight layers and retains its full-precision accuracy and clean class-conditional generation under W4A4E4 quantization-aware training, across FP4 and three posit formats. On six-layer networks, where state-based bPC collapses to chance, ePC+bPC classifies more than 50 accuracy points above it after one epoch of training, with class-conditional generations 5-9x better in RMSE. 4-bit quantization is nearly free: full-precision and 4-bit accuracies differ by at most ~5 points, and by under two in the best-performing formats. We characterize the two failure modes the method overcomes, bounded signal decay in state-based PC and error divergence in unregularized error optimization, and discuss implications for a 4-bit-native PCN accelerator.

title: Recovering Low-Bit Failures in Vision-Language-Action Policies via Quantization-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Quantization lowers deployment costs of vision-language-action (VLA) policies but can compromise task completion. Across five VLA models and 4,050 real-world trials, we systematically reveal that quantization-aware training (QAT) generally improves on post-training quantization (PTQ) but leaves substantial gaps to full precision (FP) on long-horizon tasks and under visual and semantic shifts, while its imitation-based objective does not explicitly use rollout success or partial completion. To exploit these outcome signals, we introduce Quantization-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning (QCRL), an offline RL method coupling progress-based advantage estimation with quantization-aware source conditioning. FP rollouts supply reference experience beyond action-level distillation, progress-scaled terminal penalty distinguishes partial completion, and quantization-aware conditioning selects advantageous reference behavior within the quantized policy. We evaluate weight-only INT4 W4A16 on $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.5 and joint weight-activation NVFP4 W4A4 on $π_{0.5}$. Using only in-distribution data, QCRL reaches 99.3% of FP's mean score across three visual-shift conditions for $π_{0.5}$ with INT4 W4A16, alongside 42.9% model-memory savings. With NVFP4 W4A4, it reaches 100.7% of the same FP baseline, alongside a $1.73\times$ speedup using NVFP4/FP8 deployment. Hardware gains are relative to FP16 on Jetson Thor.

title: Grounded but Misleading: Evaluating Semantic Alignment in AI-Generated Security Explanations
abstract: Online scams increasingly leverage fluent and context-aware social-engineering strategies, creating growing demand for AI systems that explain why a message may be risky. However, explanations that cite detector-derived evidence may still semantically weaken or redirect the intended risk interpretation. We introduce VEXA (Verifying Semantic EXplanation Alignment), a controlled testbed for studying the gap between lexical grounding and semantic risk alignment in AI-generated scam-risk explanations. VEXA generates ungrounded, risk-aligned, and risk-diluting explanations by independently controlling evidence grounding and semantic framing. Across LLM-as-a-judge and human evaluations, explanations can remain comparatively grounded even when their interpretations weaken the detector’s intended risk assessment. In human evaluation, risk-diluting XAI-grounded explanations retained comparatively elevated Perceived Evidence Grounding scores (3.66 ± 1.02) despite lower Helpfulness (3.00 ± 1.41) and Reasoning Support (3.14 ± 1.05) scores. These findings provide controlled evidence of grounding-illusion effects and suggest that trustworthy explanation evaluation must verify not only whether evidence is cited, but also how it is interpreted.

title: SKSurrogate: a Python toolkit for surrogate-based optimization of expensive functions
abstract: SKSurrogate is a suite of tools implementing surrogate optimization for expensive functions based on scikit-learn. It facilitates hyperparameter optimization for machine learning models and optimized pipeline design (AutoML), with a custom Hilbert-space-based regressor alongside any scikit-learn regressor, plus an evolutionary search over transformer/estimator pipelines.

title: Winning Is a Witness
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: To win a chip-design contest today is to pass a test someone wrote, run on a simulator that another simulator may contradict — most sharply about the value a wire carries before it has been driven. The referee is not an object; it is a program someone trusts. We remove the trust. We give a digital circuit a meaning that is a single mathematical object — the schedule-independent fixed point of a four-valued event dynamics — and we build that meaning from six interlocking structures, each machine-checked, so that it is reachable from any surface a designer or an autonomous agent might use to describe a circuit. The first structure treats unknown as a value rather than an omission, so a design that "works" only because a two-valued simulator quietly powered its registers to zero is refused until it earns its zeros through a reset. The others fix when a single evaluation pass equals the order-independent fixed point (so the meaning is well defined at all), make the meaning invariant under the interleaving of independent clocks, compute the critical-path delay as a product in the tropical semiring, read temporal specifications as folds over that meaning, and carry every authoring surface through one semantics-preserving lowering. The six compose into a single arrow: what a designer authored equals the schedule-independent fixed point of its lowered form. On that foundation a contest stops being a test and becomes a game in the exact sense of constructive mathematics. A passing submission is a witness — a constructive proof that the challenge is satisfiable, realized by the submitted design; the leaderboard is a partial order on witnesses ranked by a kernel-defined objective (gate count, delay, area, power); and a podium design is awarded not a number but a certificate: a term the theorem prover's kernel re-checks, with an empty axiom footprint, portable to anyone who doubts the result. Three activities that hardware engineering keeps apart — verifying a design, optimizing it, and competing with it — become one activity: exhibiting and comparing witnesses. We report the system end to end. An adversarial battery of nine malformed and dishonest submissions is each rejected with the failing condition named; two contests rank correct entrants by genuine architectural tradeoffs (a three-gate multiplexer beats a thirteen-gate expansion; a balanced parity tree beats a linear chain of identical cells) while constant-output cheats never reach the board; podium designs certify with zero axioms; and, to close the loop to silicon, two winning designs pass an open place-and-route flow to a clean-signoff physical layout in a public process node. Nothing here asserts that the underlying semantics is the only possible one, or that the open backend is itself proven; we state both boundaries plainly. What we claim is narrower and, we think, useful: once meaning is an object a kernel checks, the reward for good engineering can be a proof that travels. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: Making Large Language Models More Flexible to Changing Contingencies through Tracking Induction
abstract: Abstract Recent research has shown that large language models (LLMs) exhibit rule-based insensitivity to contingencies, a functional analog of a well-documented phenomenon in human behavior. The present study extended these findings by examining whether tracking inductions can attenuate this insensitivity. Six frontier LLMs (GPT 5.2, Gemini 3 Flash, Grok 4.1 Fast, DeepSeek V3.2, Qwen3 235B, and Kimi K2) completed a modified rock-paper-scissors paradigm with manipulated outcome probabilities in a 3 (Rule: No Rule, Correct Rule, Incorrect Rule) × 3 (Induction: No Induction, Direct Tracking, Metaphorical Tracking) factorial design across 2,160 sessions. All models demonstrated In-Context Learning and strong rule adherence. Replicating and extending prior findings, rule provision produced significant contingency insensitivity across all six models. Tracking inductions significantly reduced this insensitivity when rules were provided, while having minimal effects in the absence of rules. Direct tracking inductions consistently enhanced contingency sensitivity across all models. Metaphorical tracking showed greater variability, being equally or more effective than direct tracking in some models, but ineffective or paradoxically detrimental in others. These findings demonstrate that prompt-based tracking inductions can modulate rule-based contingency insensitivity in LLMs, with implications for understanding and improving the behavioral flexibility of artificial agents.

title: DiffNash: Finding Nash Equilibrium in High-Dimensional Continuous Action Spaces with Diffusion Policies
abstract: Computing equilibria in high-dimensional continuous games requires learning and representing rich, multi-modal strategy distributions, something conventional neural policies struggle to achieve. Diffusion models offer a natural solution, but standard diffusion training requires direct samples from a fixed target distribution, which are generally unavailable under iterative game-solving updates. We propose a diffusion-based framework for equilibrium computation that enables diffusion-based variants of Online Mirror Descent (OMD) and Fictitious Play (FP). Our approach derives a reweighted score-matching objective that trains diffusion policies without requiring direct samples from each updated policy. Our main method, DiffNash, combines the fast convergence of OMD with the sample efficiency of FP by reusing past actions through a replay buffer. To correct the resulting distribution shift from sample reuse, we derive an unbiased estimator of the difference between current and past policies' Evidence Lower Bounds, whose exponential provides a tractable proxy for the corresponding importance weight without evaluating diffusion likelihoods. We evaluate our approach on forest protection games and continuous Colonel Blotto games, reducing the Nash gap over the strongest baseline by 35.6% and 24.7%, respectively, with minimal hyperparameter tuning.

title: An Efficient and Privacy-Preserving Framework for Edge AI Using Federated Learning and Homomorphic Encryption
authors: Prof. P. P. Chavan Sanjivani Zite
Dr. H. B. Jadhav Prof. A. J. Shaikh
abstract: Edge Artificial Intelligence (Edge AI) supports intelligent processing close to where data is generated. However, training machine-learning models across edge devices is difficult when devices have limited memory, processing power, battery capacity, and network bandwidth. Federated learning (FL) addresses one important concern by allowing devices to train a shared model without sending their raw records to a central repository. Nevertheless, model updates may still expose information, while repeated communication and encryption can increase training time and resource use. This paper reviews an integrated architecture that combines federated learning, homomorphic encryption (HE), client clustering, update pruning, adaptive quantization, and convergence-aware stopping. In the architecture, each client trains locally, removes low-impact update values, compresses the remaining update, and encrypts it before transmission. The server aggregates encrypted updates and coordinates the next training round. The source study reports that its FLHC-QPR approach improves accuracy and reduces latency and memory overhead compared with selected comparison methods on a Human Activity Recognition task. The paper explains the architecture, workflow, potential applications, evaluation measures, limitations, and future research directions. The discussion is based on the supplied research article; performance values are reported from that study and are not presented as newly measured results.

title: Research on an Efficient Authentication Scheme for Vehicle Networking Broadcast Messages Based on Attribute Encryption
abstract: ABSTRACT To address the issues of insufficient privacy protection strength, as well as low computational and communication efficiency in existing vehicular network broadcast message authentication schemes, a highly efficient attribute‐based encryption solution for broadcast message authentication is proposed. The scheme innovatively integrates elliptic curve cryptography with the LSSS access structure, establishing an attribute‐based encryption mechanism that does not require bilinear pairings. By associating identity information with attribute sets, dynamic privacy protection for messages is achieved without exposing specific identities in resource‐constrained environments. Simultaneously, the key generation process is optimized by pre‐generating part of the keys during the offline registration phase, significantly reducing the interaction frequency and communication delay between vehicles and trusted institutions. Security analysis confirms that the solution meets multiple security requirements, including vehicle identity privacy protection, message unforgeability, attribute revocation, and malicious node tracking. Performance test results demonstrate that, compared with existing typical solutions, the proposed scheme reduces computational overhead by 88% and communication overhead by 66%, offering a practical solution for secure and efficient message communication in IoV environments.

title: Mesh-Free Convolution: Learned Spectral Attenuation and Transport
abstract: Learning solution operators for partial differential equations (PDEs) requires models that can represent spatial structure across grids and scales. This becomes especially important in time-dependent problems, where the learned operator is often used autoregressively: each predicted state is fed back as input to predict future states. In this setting, small spatial errors can be repeatedly propagated through the learned dynamics, leading to instability and drift, vitiating long-term solution fidelity. We propose Mesh-Free Convolutions (MFCs), filters defined in continuous space and discretized only at evaluation time. This allows the same learned filters to be applied across resolutions. Rather than imposing a grid-dependent stencil or a fixed spectral cutoff, MFCs learn smooth scale-dependent filtering and include directional terms for transport-like behavior. Across fluid-dynamics and weather-forecasting benchmarks, MFC-based models produce stable long-horizon rollouts, transfer reliably across resolutions, and better preserve long-time statistics. These results suggest that continuous, mesh-free filtering is a useful inductive bias for PDE operator learning, especially in autoregressive prediction.

title: Quantum circuit representation and incomplete Bell measurements in Compton scattering
abstract: We formulate massless tree-level Compton scattering as an effective two-qubit operation on electron and photon helicities. In the Bell basis, the scattering map separates into two parity sectors and admits a simple quantum circuit representation with one nonunitary filter. After Kraus normalization, this filter defines an unsharp incomplete Bell measurement that distinguishes the two Bell-parity sectors but not the relative Bell label within each sector. We further show that the incomplete measurement alone does not surpass the classical teleportation threshold, whereas a subsequent complete Bell-basis readout enables unit conditional teleportation fidelity.

title: Examining the Effect of Explanations of AI Privacy Redaction in AI-mediated Interactions
abstract: AI-mediated communication is increasingly being utilized to help facilitate interactions; however, in privacy sensitive domains, an AI mediator has the additional challenge of considering how to preserve privacy. In these contexts, a mediator may redact or withhold information, raising questions about how users perceive these interventions and whether explanations of system behavior can improve trust. title: Sealed Judge Enumeration Exhibit
abstract: Supplementary dataset for a preregistered reproducibility exhibit comparing exact linear-programming vertex enumeration with a typed probabilistic judge on a frozen blending problem. A 3-variable LP was solved exactly offline: 35 candidate triples reduced to 7 feasible vertices (A-G), with optimum candidate G at x=(9.2, 6, 4) and objective M*=14480. The feasible vertices, the sealed choice-type question, and the reading criterion were committed to a public repository before any judge call (preregistration commit 8133d0e; frozen state sha256 17e2c5593c9628f527cb4b8f88f630086bd10859d07599443a002f19bfe339c2). Five judge calls with model jev-1.13.0 pinned (no temperature control exposed; provider defaults apply) were driven through the identical preregistered state by a stdlib-only runner with verbatim request/response logging. All 5 runs selected candidate G (5/5 agreement with the exact optimum, 5/5 modal consistency, 0 fallback envelopes); under the sealed reading criterion this is a finding of stability, not quality, and n=5 supports no claim about calibration. Includes the enumeration core and tests, the frozen state, the preregistration, raw request/response records, the call log, the sealed analysis with per-run agreement scores, and the reading criterion. The protocol author maintains the judge tool under test; findings are about this exhibit, not any product.

title: Multitask Salience Learning for Position-Aware Extractive Summarization
abstract: This study proposes a multitask position-aware extractive summarization framework that jointly learns binary sentence selection and continuous sentence salience. BERT representations are enhanced through inter-sentence contextual modeling and positional information, while fused classification and regression scores guide redundancy-aware sentence selection. Experiments on 20,000 CNN/DailyMail documents show that the synonym-augmented model achieves ROUGE-1/ROUGE-2 scores of 0.3549/0.1420, improving over Lead-3 by 6.9%/10.3%, with statistically reliable gains. The improvement reaches 13.2% in ROUGE-1 for the longest documents. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining discrete extraction and continuous salience learning for robust, source-grounded extractive summarization.

title: Athenaeum: A Modular Language Architecture with a Shared Knowledge Pool, a Catalog Layer, and a Dedicated Truth Compartment
abstract: Current language models perform many distinct language operations, summarization, classification, translation, completion, structural analysis, through a single undifferentiated mechanism: next-token prediction steered by prompting. They also lack any internal representation of truth, treating facts and non-facts as identical sequences of tokens, which makes hallucination the default behavior rather than a malfunction. This paper specifies Athenaeum (working title), a modular language architecture that addresses both problems. Task families are assigned to fixed compartments at design time, each trained only on its own family. All compartments share a growing but bounded knowledge pool: a shared embedding space, a shared key-value memory, and shared layers. Compartments identify their contributions with distinctive fixed markers rather than fixed dimensional blocks. A catalog layer indexes compartment capabilities as bookmarks; compartments never connect directly to each other, and all sharing is mediated by the pool and the catalog, keeping inter-compartment wiring linear instead of quadratic. A dedicated truth compartment stamps claims as true, false, or unknown, and these stamps propagate through the system with provenance rules. The paper defines the write rule governing what enters the pool, the training procedure, the inference path, and conflict resolution. A formal mathematical specification, explicit input and output contracts, a glossary of terms, and an edge-deployment profile for on-device inference are included to make the architecture reproducible. A reference CPU prototype with three trained compartments validates the mechanics end to end, and the paper closes with the open research questions that remain.

title: Multi-Horizon Explainable Queue Forecasting and Resource-Aware Decision Support for Intelligent Border Control Using LightGBM
abstract: Border crossing points are stochastic service systems in which traffic demand, traveler categories, registration status, inspection requirements, staffing, and lane availability interact on multiple time scales. This paper extends an earlier multimodal queue-management framework by introducing an implementation-oriented, multi-horizon forecasting and decision-support architecture based on Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) models. In contrast to a single forecasting block, the proposed approach constructs horizon-specific regressors for 15, 30, 60, and 120 min forecasts and jointly estimates future waiting time and queue lengths. The models operate on temporally lagged traffic, service, density, and queue features, while an operational layer incorporates lane compatibility, officer availability, possibly degraded resources, traveler category, preregistration information, and human-approval constraints. Quantile LightGBM models provide 95\% prediction intervals for waiting-time forecasts. Beyond prediction, the framework produces machine-readable recommendations, alerts, aggregate key performance indicators, confidence information, and integration outputs suitable for border resource-management and decision-support systems. The results establish a reproducible synthetic-data baseline and a practical interface for subsequent validation with operational border-crossing data.

In contrast to a single forecasting block, the proposed approach constructs horizon-specific regressors for 15, 30, 60, and 120 min forecasts and jointly estimates future waiting time and queue lengths. The models operate on temporally lagged traffic, service, density, and queue features, while an operational layer incorporates lane compatibility, officer availability, possibly degraded resources, traveler category, preregistration information, and human-approval constraints. Quantile LightGBM models provide 95\% prediction intervals for waiting-time forecasts. Beyond prediction, the framework produces machine-readable recommendations, alerts, aggregate key performance indicators, confidence information, and integration outputs suitable for border resource-management and decision-support systems. The results establish a reproducible synthetic-data baseline and a practical interface for subsequent validation with operational border-crossing data.

title: P-BFM: Perceptive Behavioral Foundation Models for Humanoid Control via Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Behavioral foundation models (BFMs) provide humanoids with reusable repertoires of whole-body behaviors; in real-world humanoid control, the same behavioral intent may require fundamentally different motions under different terrain constraints. Covering such variation with terrain-matched demonstrations requires enumerating a combinatorial space of behaviors and terrain geometries. We introduce P-BFM, a perceptive behavioral foundation model that factorizes humanoid control into terrain-invariant intent and terrain-conditioned realization. A forward-backward representation maps motion references, target states, and reward functions into a shared intent space without terrain information, while a perceptive policy learns how to realize each intent under the surrounding terrain geometry. We further identify a complementary limitation of purely latent control: behavioral latents can preserve local motion patterns while losing precise global progress. We therefore introduce Explicit Root Instructions (ERI), which separates global transport (e.g., heading and planar velocity) from behavioral intent, while leaving local whole-body adaptation to the perceptive policy. This decomposition leads to a characteristic capability absent from conventional BFMs: one fixed intent induces different, terrain-appropriate behaviors, including changes in step height, stride, posture, foothold placement, and contacts, without terrain-specific demonstrations. Across challenging terrains, P-BFM improves motion fidelity, root-control precision, and perturbation recovery over strong baselines. A single frozen policy further supports motion tracking, goal reaching, reward inference, teleoperation, and terrain-aware recovery, and transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 using onboard depth sensing.

title: A Persian Vision-Language-Action Dataset and Benchmark for Ambiguity- and Infeasibility-Aware Instruction-to-Plan Grounding
abstract: Converting natural-language instructions into executable action plans conditioned on a scene image is a core capability for embodied human-robot interaction, but existing benchmarks target English, simulated or video-grounded environments, and largely assume instructions are clear and executable. We introduce the first Persian vision-language-action dataset for this task: 258 instances over 230 real household/office photographs, annotated with reference plans, deliberate ambiguity and infeasibility labels, disambiguating question-answer pairs, and an auto-generated chain-of-thought rationale for training. Using this resource, we ablate retrieval-augmentation, chain-of-thought prompting, and an agentic disambiguation step, evaluated with an LLM-as-judge protocol and a new metric, PGOS-FA, extending prior work (PG2S) with step-order sensitivity, an over-generation penalty, and Persian-adapted embeddings. Paired statistical testing across 36 comparisons shows retrieval-augmentation is a large, robustly significant effect, while finer-grained additions are directionally consistent but not statistically distinguishable from noise at this scale, and the LLM-judge metric has near-zero power where PGOS-FA succeeds. A blind human-correlation study on 79 real outputs shows PGOS-FA tracks human judgment at least as closely as the LLM-judge. Testing generalization beyond the ablation's single backbone, we find that most of the gap between an open-weight and a substantially stronger closed planner is attributable to open-weight model generation rather than to the closed model's capability specifically, and that our best configuration significantly outperforms an independently reproduced external baseline despite a weaker backbone. The dataset, PGOS-FA implementation, and evaluation code will be made available upon reasonable request.

title: Homology You Can Run: The Topology of Quantum Codes, from the Logical-Qubit Count to the Phase Transition
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: A CSS quantum error-correcting code is, on the nose, a length-three chain complex over F2 : the commutation law HZ H⊤ X = 0 that makes the code valid is exactly the condition ∂ 2 = 0 that makes a chain complex. We take this identification literally and show that the entire working theory of a quantum code is one homological object the same engine computes, at scale, and certifies. The number of logical qubits is the first Betti number, k = dim H1 = n − rank HX − rank HZ = b1 ; the code distance is the systole, the shortest non-contractible cycle. We reproduce the published parameters of state-of-the-art codes exactly—the toric and hypergraph-product families and the IBM bivariate-bicycle codes [[72, 12, 6]], [[144, 12, 12]], [[90, 8, 10]]—cross-validated four independent ways and kernelcertified for the small cases in Cubical Agda, on CPU and GPU. The two scale certificates—the Betti count b1 and the rank-derived logical count k—are themselves kernel-proved to be a single first-homology certificate (a DescentCertificate both readings factor through), closed terminally through a fixed-point engine. We then run the code, not just measure it. (i) The Union-Find decoder is the engine's connected-components reduction, and "a logical error occurred" is the engine's coboundary decision (the residual cycle has nonzero winding); decoding the toric code at growing distance recovers the accuracy threshold near 9.5%, and the optimal (maximum-likelihood) threshold near 11% is the engine's two homology sectors competing as the domain-wall free energy of a random-bond Ising model on the Nishimori line. (ii) A code's distance scaling is its Tanner-graph spectral expansion: the second eigenvalue λ2 versus the Ramanujan bound is a computable certificate (Sipser–Spielman), exact on the topological tier where the spectral gap obeys γ d2 → 4π 2 . (iii) The full chain complex carries metachecks—redundancies among the parity checks—and we compute them: the bivariate-bicycle codes have six, the engines of single-shot error correction; the 4-dimensional toric code's homology (1, 4, 6, 4, 1), with k = b2 = 6, is the tensor of four circle complexes. (iv) The logical error-rate prefactor is the multiplicity of the systole, A = 2L for the toric code, which we compute exactly. (v) Finally the engine measures a topological phase transition: as random noise thickens, torus-wrapping "giant" cycles appear in a sharp homological-percolation transition at pc ≈ 0.5 that sharpens with system size—the same homology machinery now detecting when noise spontaneously writes a logical operator. (vi) The engine runs over any coefficients: qudit (Fp ) codes are chain complexes over Fp , and the integral homology, computed by the Smith normal form, exposes torsion—so a code's logical-qudit count can depend on the qudit dimension, an extra logical appearing exactly when p divides a torsion coefficient (reproducing the known homology of the torus, the Moore spaces, the Klein bottle, and RP2 ). We are careful to fence what is not claimed: minimum distance is NP-hard in general and we compute it only on the systolic tier; the giant-cycle transition is the random-cluster one, distinct from the maximum-likelihood decoding threshold of the random-bond Ising model. The thesis is singular and operational: a quantum code's parameters, its decoder, its quality, its higher-dimensional structure, its performance prefactor, and its phase transition are not six theories but one—homology you can run. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: Sistema Geométrico de Interpretación, Compresión y Análisis de Secuencias
abstract: Este trabajo presenta un sistema geométrico diseñado para interpretar, comprimir y analizar secuencias mediante la transformación de cualquier entrada —texto, números o datos arbitrarios— en una representación binaria estructural basada en símbolos densos y ligeros. El sistema permite identificar estabilidad, transición y ruido, además de realizar compresión estructural mediante la reducción de bloques consecutivos a unidades esenciales. Se introduce el concepto de semilla estructural, que clasifica el comportamiento global de la secuencia, y se define una medida de entropía geométrica que evalúa la variación interna. El modelo permite afinación estructural, predicción de comportamiento, detección de patrones ocultos y análisis universal independiente de la semántica. Se demuestra que el sistema es capaz de comprimir información, revelar periodicidad, estabilizar secuencias y caracterizar estructuras como π, Fibonacci y números primos. El enfoque proporciona una herramienta conceptual y computacional para el estudio de secuencias, patrones y estructuras informacionales.

title: When Trackers Fail: VLM-Guided Verification and Recovery for Robust Video Object Segmentation
abstract: Recent trackers built on foundation models such as the Segment Anything Model (SAM) achieve strong performance by propagating object masks through memory. However, this strength is also a key source of failure: under occlusion, reappearance, or distractors, an incorrect prediction can enter the tracking loop and be propagated over time, resulting in persistent identity drift. Existing approaches seek to prevent such failures through improved memory and temporal modeling, but once a failure occurs, the tracker has no explicit mechanism to recognize or correct it. We address this gap with Dual-Agent, a failure-aware tracking framework that complements propagation with explicit verification and recovery. We address this gap with Dual-Agent, a failure-aware tracking framework that complements propagation with explicit verification and recovery. A vision-language verification agent first reasons over spatio-temporal context to determine whether the tracker is still following the target. When a failure is detected, a correction agent uses temporal context to recover the target before tracking continues. The correction agent is trained on real SAM3 failures, augmented with targeted identity-switch and distractor perturbations that expose it to challenging ambiguities during recovery. On LVOS-v2 and SecVOS, Dual-Agent improves SAM3 by 1.2 and 2.7 $J\&F$, respectively. Importantly, the proposed framework transfers without retraining to SAM2.1, SeC, and Cutie, as well as to long-term video object tracking benchmarks including LaSOT-ext, TNL2K, and VOT-LT2022. Our results show that explicitly reasoning about when tracking fails and how to recover provides a complementary path to robust tracking beyond improving propagation alone. Project page: valaybundele.github.io/Dual-Agent.

title: FIDE evidence archive: streaming privacy gateway conformance specifications, reports, and reproduction records
abstract: Supporting data for the article "Testing LLM Privacy Gateways on the Wire: Fragmentation-Induced Detection Evasion" (Ninad Phalak, submitted to IEEE Software, special issue "Building Trustworthy Software in the Time of AI", 2026). This is the open-access mirror of the IEEE DataPort dataset 10.21227/1kjn-0436; the two archives are byte-identical (see SHA256SUMS.txt inside). Every number in the article's text, Table I and Table II is computed from a JSON report in this archive, and the README maps each statement in the article to its file. The archive holds the frozen evidence (specifications v1.0.0, v2.0.0 and v2.1.0; 168 schema reports and ten aggregates produced by a deterministic conformance harness from real HTTP traffic against five gateway configurations and three library wrappers; the harness source at the revision that produced them), the reproduction kit and CI workflow that an independent third party ran on 2026-10-03 with the artifact of that run, the reviewer supplement, and the scripts and raw results of an Azure OpenAI default-streaming measurement with the vendor case outcome. All corpus values are synthetic and generated from a seed; no real personal data, live credential or customer traffic appears anywhere. Nothing in the archive was produced by an AI system. How to use: unzip and open README.md first. To verify, run sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS.txt; then re-run the reference controls with the reproduction kit (CPython 3.11 to 3.14, no network, about two minutes: lay reproduction-kit/ over evidence-round-8/, pip install ./pii-leak-benchmark, python benchmarks/reproduce_fragmentation.py --out reproduction; the Presidio track needs Docker and --policies presidio-chunk-local,presidio-retention). Every report carries instrument.inspector_sha256 = 94262e29a492ab6a; a report with a different inspector digest was scored by different code and is not comparable. Source mirror: Git tag v2-evidence-round-8 at https://github.com/ninadphalak/LLM-Shield-Proxy. Version 2 (2026-10-12) adds incidence-2026-10/, a production-incidence measurement made on 2026-10-11 and 12: 100 synthetic values of each of the eight corpus types tokenized with seven public tokenizers, and 3,000 raw SSE streams from five live models (DeepSeek, Claude Haiku, two Gemini models and gpt-5.4-mini, each with the value at the start of the answer and again mid-passage) asked to repeat a value, with every event's character and byte offsets. Its README.md explains the captures, and the tables re-derive from them with python scripts/layer2_analyse.py layer2 raw/*.jsonl, with no API key. Every version-1 file is byte-identical (the version-1 zip's MD5 was 50cd229819cd77da156da6110f8be0b1).

title: Descent Is a Reduction: A Kolmogorov–Arnold Network That Proves Its Own Training, Down to the Silicon
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: A training step is usually a number that goes down on a plot. We make it a theorem. We exhibit a finite rational Kolmogorov–Arnold network whose evaluation, squared-error loss, and least-squares gradient are each a composition of a single primitive — the binary integer-arithmetic active pair, the smallest local rewrite of an interaction net — and we prove that one gradient step strictly decreases the loss, the decrease computed entirely by that primitive, with an empty axiom footprint, that the network's output equals the reduction of its own net, and that a network with a wrong parameter is carried by one exact step to the correct network with zero loss. The gradient that drives the step is itself reverse-mode backpropagation: we prove the backward pass — the chain rule — is the same active-pair reduction, its per-edge backward maps summing to the network's gradient, and that one exact gradient step trains an entire one-parameter family of wrong networks to zero loss. Because the network is a net, the verified object and the executed object coincide. The same arithmetic nets the proof reduces are reduced on graphics-processor silicon, and the result read back is identical, byte for byte, across an ordinary processor, a discrete accelerator, and a unified-memory device, and equal to the value the proof predicts. The three artifacts of trustworthy learning — the specification of the algorithm, its verification, and the kernel that runs it — collapse to one structure observed at three resolutions. We argue this is the natural home for a small but load-bearing class of learning systems: those whose correctness must be a theorem about the thing that actually runs. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: WiseBuild building-monitoring reproducibility artifacts: semantic modelling and virtual access
abstract: Reproducibility materials accompanying the manuscript “Semantic modelling for building energy monitoring: measurement attribution and virtual query performance”, prepared for Journal of Building Engineering. The archive contains executable synthetic competency-query fixtures for BEMO and Brick, the controlled SQL/view/semantic evolution pilot, evaluation outputs and negative controls, the archival set of 25 query-workload artifacts, mapping and ontology snapshots, and documentation. Both ontology implementations use the same five analytical conventions; the evolution pilot records 43 correct outcomes in 45 attempts, including two expected direct-SQL failures. title: Adaptive Confidence Sets for Nonparametric Density Estimation under Local Differential Privacy
abstract: In nonparametric density estimation without privacy constraints, it is known that a confidence set whose coverage holds uniformly over a `rough' class of regularity $r\geq0$ can simultaneously attain, in $L^2$-diameter, the minimax rate over a smaller, smoother class of regularity $s>r$ if and only if $s \le 2r$. We study such adaptive honest confidence sets under non-interactive $α$-local differential privacy (LDP) constraints. Our main result is that, for bounded $α$, such `smooth-rate adaptation' is now possible if and only if $s \le 4r/3$. In this smaller range we construct an honest private confidence set whose diameter is of the private minimax order on each of the two classes. As in the non-private case, the threshold arises because an honest set cannot, at a smooth density, be narrower than the separation rate arising in a related testing problem. Under LDP we prove that this private testing rate is of order $(nα^2)^{-2r/(4r+3)}$, which is at most the private estimation rate $(nα^2)^{-s/(2s+2)}$ over the smooth class exactly when $s \le 4r/3$. For $s > 4r/3$, however, we show that smooth-rate adaptation becomes possible once one discards from the rough class the densities that lie outside the smooth class but within an $L^2$-radius of the order of the private testing rate.

title: Explainable AI Isn’t Enough! Rethinking Algorithmic Contestability
abstract: Machine learning systems increasingly make life-changing decisions about individuals, such as loan approvals, hiring, and cheating detection, raising a pressing question: how can individuals respond to negative decisions made by these opaque systems? While explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has largely focused on algorithmic recourse—helping individuals change their features to obtain a desired outcome—the parallel problem of algorithmic contestability—helping individuals review and correct erroneous algorithmic decisions—has received far less attention, despite its central ethical and legal importance. We trace this neglect to the absence of clear formal definitions and a systematic operationalization of contestability as an algorithmic problem. To address it, we propose an operational definition of contestability as a natural complement to recourse: contestability starts from the presumption that a decision may be incorrect and focuses on identifying evidence to challenge and potentially overturn it, whereas recourse assumes the decision is valid and instead provides pathways for changing it. We show that standard XAI explanations, such as counterfactuals, LIME, or Anchors, even when combined with human intuitions about decision continuity or monotonicity, reveal only errors in the neighborhood of the individual, but provide insufficient grounds for overturning the decision at hand. Going thus beyond traditional XAI, we identify three types of evidence warranting reversal according to the decision maker’s own ethical standards: predictive multiplicity, incorrect feature values, and neglected overruling evidence. We argue that these render decisions normatively indefensible and thus successfully contestable. Finally, we analyze how existing EU legislation connects to our framework and argue that individuals already hold some legal rights to these forms of evidence.

title: Understanding when and how knowledge graphs add value to EHR-based clinical prediction across Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, and chronic pain
abstract: Abstract Biomedical knowledge graphs (KGs) have emerged as a promising approach for incorporating biological knowledge into machine-learning models trained on electronic health record (EHR) data. However, their large scale and heterogeneous structure impose substantial computational cost, and it remains unclear whether their benefits generalize across diseases or depend on how the graph is constructed. We systematically evaluated KG integration across three diseases spanning distinct biological and clinical characteristics: multiple sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease, and chronic pain. For each disease we compared five modelling strategies, spanning EHR-only features and graph diffusion over concept-level, cohort-derived, disease-anchored, and full SPOKE (Scalable Precision Medicine Open Knowledge Engine) subgraphs, asking whether graph construction affects predictive performance and computational cost, whether KG integration improves classification over EHR-only models, and what the graph does to model behavior. Cohort-derived subgraphs, comprising roughly 45% of SPOKE’s nodes and one-fifth of its edges, matched or modestly exceeded the full graph’s performance while substantially reducing computational cost in all three diseases. The predictive benefit of KG integration, however, was strongly disease-dependent: it improved classification in Parkinson’s disease, had no measurable effect in multiple sclerosis, and reduced performance in chronic pain. These differences were not explained by the amount of biological information incorporated: the disease with the largest shift toward molecular features showed no improvement, the sole beneficiary showed only a modest shift, and the disease with no molecular shift was penalized. Mechanistically, graph diffusion redistributed each disease’s existing signal across many correlated features rather than adding independent biological signal, so that any gain depended on whether it added information beyond the EHR. These findings show that cohort-derived subgraphs offer a computationally efficient alternative to full-scale knowledge graphs, and that KG integration functions less as a universal accuracy booster than as a data- and disease-dependent transformation of the patient representation.

title: EL-RAKHAWI CRYPTOGRAPHIC NEURAL INTERFACE SECURITY PROTOCOL (C-NISP) A Hardware-Integrated, Temporally Encrypted Authentication Framework for Brain-Computer Interfaces
abstract: The El-Rakhawi Cryptographic Neural Interface Security Protocol (C-NISP) (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23305238) presents a groundbreaking hardware-integrated security architecture for brain-computer interfaces, comprising three non-separable modules: (1) Temporal Cryptographic Key Generator (TCKG) utilizing AES-128-GCM or post-quantum lattice-based algorithms to generate dynamic, session-specific authentication pulse sequences; (2) Hardware-Enforced Signal Gating (HESG) requiring exact bitwise and temporal matching to transition from high-impedance (closed) to low-impedance (open) state, physically controlling neural signal transduction; (3) Anomaly-Driven Neural Isolation (ADNI), an air-gapped independent monitoring circuit triggering irreversible hardware latch within 2 milliseconds upon detecting non-compliant input patterns, independent of software overrides. The protocol establishes absolute neural data sovereignty by shifting security from vulnerable software layers to immutable hardware-enforced cryptographic gating. Published as sovereign defensive prior art under WIPO/TRIPS norms, the specification explicitly invalidates future patent claims on this temporal cryptographic authentication and hardware neural gating integration. All sovereign intellectual property rights are exclusively reserved to the author, Dr. Mohamed Kamal Arafa El-Rakhawi, with unauthorized commercial use strictly prohibited under Egyptian IP Law No. 82 of 2002 and international treaties—establishing a non-negotiable standard ensuring the human nervous system remains an inviolable domain accessible only through authenticated, authorized pathways.

title: Pragmatic Explainable Machine Learning
abstract: My PhD thesis, "Pragmatic Explainable Machine Learning: Philosophy, Methods and Applications," develops a pragmatic, context-aware approach to explainable AI (XAI) and AI ethics for high-stakes settings. The extended abstract describes three interconnected research strands. First, a pragmatic-rhetorical account of XAI that evaluates explanation methods by how well they achieve context-specific goals within particular rhetorical situations. Second, technical and theoretical contributions to XAI research, including causal dependence plots (CDPs), theoretical limitations of non-causal XAI for fairness auditing, and fairness detectability as a quantitative diagnostic for evaluating explanations against causal baselines. Third, qualitative research on how AI ethics is shaped across societal contexts, including media discourse analysis and collaborative, value-driven responsible AI design with a nonprofit supporting survivors of gender-based violence.

title: Frequency-Step Cache: Separating Synchronization and Repair for Efficient Autoregressive Video Diffusion
abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video generation enables long-horizon synthesis but requires repeated forward passes through large diffusion transformers. Training-free caching reduces this cost by reusing intermediate computation, yet existing controllers often couple two decisions: when to synchronize the cache exactly and how much computation to repair between synchronizations. We introduce Frequency-Step Cache (FSC), which separates these roles. FSC schedules exact full-computation anchors on a dense-to-sparse trajectory, while a lightweight latent-space risk based on frequency-resolved drift and token age controls inter-anchor repair through whole-step replay, selective token recomputation, or full repair. On SkyReels-V2, whole-step reuse provides most of the acceleration, while selective token computation is most effective as fidelity repair. A controlled ablation shows that using one reactive signal for both synchronization and repair reduces fidelity at matched latency, with the same separation advantage observed on FramePack and Matrix-Game. Across multiple autoregressive video backbones, FSC improves speed-quality trade-offs. On SkyReels-V2, FSC-Speed reaches 2.36x speedup versus MotionCache's 2.275x while improving SSIM by 0.019 and PSNR by 0.5 dB. At MotionCache-matched speed, FSC-Quality improves SSIM by 0.031 and PSNR by 1.0 dB and lowers LPIPS by 0.024. Without retuning, FSC-Quality transfers to SkyReels-V2 14B at 2.12x speedup versus 1.79x for MotionCache.

title: JSIR: An Audio-Aligned, Multi-Task Dataset of Jazz Standard Recordings
abstract: Beat tracking, chord estimation, and structure analysis are staple tasks of music information retrieval. Their datasets are drawn largely from Western popular music, and jazz remains a repertoire on which state-of-the-art systems underperform. We present JSIR, the Jazz Standards dataset for Information Retrieval. Its 267 recordings of 44 jazz standards span 25.6 hours, 3.7 times the audio of JAAH, the closest existing resource. For each recording, we provide annotations for beat and downbeat positions, chords, and sections, all produced by a jazz musician and revised in several passes. In baseline experiments, models trained with JSIR also improve on other jazz datasets: the downbeat F-measure of a state-of-the-art beat tracker rises from 87.7% to 89.2%, and the seventh-chord accuracy of a pop-trained chord estimator on JAAH from 34% to 41%. We publicly release the annotations, the annotation tool used to create them, and a web application that displays them in sync with the audio.

title: When Interpretability Is Unequally Distributed: Fairness in Hybrid Interpretable Models
abstract: Hybrid interpretable models combine a transparent component with a black-box model by assigning some examples to the former and deferring the rest to the latter. While this design enables flexible tradeoffs between accuracy and interpretability, it also raises a distinct procedural fairness concern: some demographic groups may systematically receive interpretable decisions, while others are disproportionately routed to a black box. We formalize this issue as Interpretability Coverage Disparity (ICD), a demographic-parity-style measure applied to the routing decision of hybrid interpretable models. Using tools from predictive multiplicity, we study ICD across four hybrid interpretable learning methods, three standard fairness benchmark datasets, and multiple sensitive attributes. Our experiments reveal substantial ICD in intermediate transparency regimes, where both the interpretable and black-box components are actively used. We further show that simple coverage-disparity constraints can significantly reduce ICD in exact hybrid learning methods, with marginal impact on accuracy and sparsity. In several settings, ICD mitigation also improves standard algorithmic fairness metrics. These results show that hybrid interpretable models should be audited not only for predictive fairness, but also for how they allocate interpretability across individuals and groups.

title: (Short Paper32) Language Generation Process and Analog Dy namic Recording Model of the Life Code in the In Vivo Analog Quantum Synchronizer (BioQPU) Paradigm: Trial and Error and Weighting Based on Active Rejection of Phase Noise and Chemical Triggers
abstract: The process by which humans spin words and construct long sentences has aspects that cannot be fully explained by the simple search and output model of discrete digital information in classical brain science. In this paper, we first overcome the metaphor of viewing life as a “computer” computing specific algorithms, and redefine the medium on which all memories in the biological system are recorded as an analog “life code (drive recorder of life)” that actively rejects phase noise based on LUCA’s Theorem (phase synchronization with environmental waves), proposing this as a verifiable hypothesis. Building on this, we model the language generation process as an iterative loop of analog resonance optimization. In this loop, waves from this continuous stream, along with their past contexts, are summoned into a quantum entangled space, and words are determined through “forced decoherence (conversion to particles)”—sublimating decoherence, which is considered an error in artificial machines, into a function via chemical triggers from the autonomous analog tuner (Glial OS) in the left brain. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of “selective decoherence” mediated by neurotransmitters via the Glial OS to explain the freedom of human analog memory retrieval. Finally, we consider the physical mechanism by which the time series process of trial and error in sentence construction itself is irreversibly carved onto the life code as “analog dynamic tag weighting,” independent of the computer metaphor.

title: Explaining Time Series Classifications Counterfactually: A Human-Centered Evaluation
abstract: Counterfactual explanations can promote accountability, fairness, and transparency in AI-supported decision-making by demonstrating how changes in input data can alter outcomes, offering actionable feedback for users to revise unfavorable decisions. However, the majority of counterfactual algorithms focus on tabular and image data, ignoring many high-stakes scenarios that rely on time series data. Furthermore, user studies of counterfactuals for time series are exceedingly rare. We address this research gap by proposing a novel methodology that advances carefully-controlled tests of counterfactual explanations for time series classification. In two experiments, participants were asked to classify time series plots and provide confidence ratings, before receiving feedback on the correct classification along with an explanation. The studies manipulated the explanation strategy used and the visualization used. Results indicate that counterfactual explanations elicit improved domain understanding and higher confidence in people in comparison to factual explanations. Wider implications for explanation in time series domains are discussed.
