title: Testing Central Structure for Complex Networks
abstract: Centrality measures rank nodes even when the observed differences can be explained by ordinary structural variation. We therefore study a preceding question: whether a network contains a statistically identifiable central structure at all. We formulate this question as a network-level hypothesis testing issue using the adjacency spectral radius as the test statistic and estimate an empirical p-value from randomized networks generated under a specified null model. The framework is evaluated using G(N,M), Chung-Lu, and two implementations of the configuration model on simulated benchmarks and 55 real networks. Controlled experiments further vary the number and connection weights of designated central nodes while holding network size and density fixed. The results show a clear negative association between central-structure strength and the empirical p-value. They also demonstrate that rejection decisions depend substantially on the structural properties preserved by the null model: the detected network sets are not simply nested across models.

title: Video-Based Sexual Harassment Detection Using Fine-Tuned Video Transformers
abstract: Sexual harassment represents a pervasive societal challenge, with a substantial proportion of incidents remaining unreported due to insufficient evidence and delayed intervention mechanisms. Smart surveillance systems capable of detecting such incidents in real-time could assist law enforcement and serve as a deterrent. However, video-based harassment detection poses significant challenges, including variations in clothing, illumina- tion, partial occlusions, low resolution, and diverse camera view- points. Despite its social importance, this problem has received limited research attention, primarily due to the scarcity of large- scale annotated video datasets. To address this gap, we extend the Sexual Harassment Video (SHV) dataset to 600 short video clips sourced from YouTube and annotated into harassment and non-harassment categories using consistent labeling guidelines. We fine-tune three state-of-the-art video transformer models, VideoMAE, ViViT, and TimeSformer, pretrained on Kinetics- 400, for binary harassment classification. Experimental results show that all three models achieve competitive classification performance, with TimeSformer attaining the highest test accu- racy of 92.27%, outperforming VideoMAE 91.71% and ViViT 91.16% on the extended SHV test set. Our analysis reveals that performance is notably influenced by dataset size, video quality, frame sampling strategy, and model architecture. This work presents a comprehensive evaluation of modern video transformers for this sensitive real-world task.

title: Scalable and Explainable AI Architectures for Intelligent Decision-Support Systems: Systematic Literature Review Protocol
abstract: Protocol of a systematic literature review, registered before the searches are run. The review maps how AI-based decision-support systems integrate data pipelines, machine-learning and relational inference, explainability, decision-support interaction, and human oversight, to ground a reference architecture for scalable and explainable decision support. It follows Kitchenham and Charters (2007) and will be reported according to PRISMA 2020. The protocol defines three research questions (layers integrated; how explainability and human oversight are realized; levels of evaluation), six databases (Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, arXiv, OpenAIRE Graph) plus Google Scholar and citation searching, five supervisor-approved search strings with five documented supplementary strings and their pilot results, eligibility criteria, a double-screened 20% sample with Cohen's kappa, a five-item quality assessment, a data-extraction form, and the synthesis plan. Appendix A gives the exact query for every database.

title: Ai-powered Chess Analysis System for Skill Development: a Case Study Aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals
abstract: Chess players often face difficulties in identifying their mistakes, understanding positional weaknesses, and improving their playing skills through traditional training methods. This research proposes an AI-powered chess analysis system that uses chess engine evaluations and game analysis to identify errors, assess player performance, and recommend personalised training activities. The study also explores how AI-based chess learning can support Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by promoting accessible, personalised, and technology-driven learning. The proposed system aims to provide a structured approach to chess skill development through data-driven feedback and targeted practice.

title: We Need Explanation Cards to Connect Explanation Algorithms to the Real World
abstract: Algorithmic explanations are intended to help stakeholders understand opaque algorithmic decisions, but in practice, they often fall short. First, the meaning of algorithmic explanations is often not what one might intuitively expect, so expert knowledge is required to interpret them correctly. Second, recent work has shown that popular explanation algorithms are uninformative about the behavior of complex decision functions. Together, these issues create a gap between what explanations appear to convey and what they actually provide. In this work, we propose Explanation Cards for Explanation Algorithms, which augment standard explanations with complementary information about robustness and validity, as well as clear instructions for interpretation. The complementary information can render otherwise uninformative explanations practically useful, while also helping to detect cases where they are not. Importantly, the interpretation instructions in explanation cards shift responsibility from users to providers: Rather than expecting users to recognize what can and cannot be concluded from an explanation, providers must make this explicit upfront. Using counterfactual explanations and SHAP as examples, we demonstrate how providers can construct explanation cards and that these cards provide users with the guidance needed for sound interpretation. We further argue that explanation cards provide a practical framework for adhering to the explainability provisions of the EU AI Act. Overall, explanation cards are a significant step toward making explanation algorithms fit for real-world use cases.

title: RINO: Renormalization Group Distillation with No Labels
abstract: Supervised machine learning in high-energy physics (HEP) requires training on labeled simulations of particle collisions, which are known to be unfaithful to the underlying physics. This leads to significant inaccuracies and biases in the transfer of trained models to real data, limiting the power of deep learning methods. Self-supervised learning (SSL) is a promising alternative for pretraining directly on real, unlabeled data. However, existing techniques largely operate with inductive biases inspired by domains such as images and natural language. We propose RINO (Renormalization Group DIstillation with NO Labels), which, for the first time, exploits the fundamentally multi-scale renormalization group structure of high-energy jet formation as a physically grounded source of SSL views. We define teacher-student representations across energy scales using different levels of hierarchical clustering, aligned via DINO-style self-distillation. To mirror the background-dominated nature of real collider data, RINO pretrains exclusively on jets from quantum chromodynamics (QCD) processes and is evaluated on out-of-distribution (OOD) transfer to rare signal classes. In our controlled data-efficiency study, RINO matches fully supervised training on JetNet after finetuning on only 1% of the labeled data. With the full labeled dataset, RINO improves OOD classification accuracy on top-quark jets by 5.9% and, without retraining, improves AUC on the unseen Higgs boson decay channel $H \to 4q$ by 4.1% over the strongest SSL baseline. Scale-structure diagnostics reveal that DINO-style self-distillation permits our backbone to retain scale-dependent structure. Ablation studies show that this accounts for an 8.6% OOD accuracy gap with respect to alternative SSL paradigms such as SimCLR. Code is available at https://github.com/zichunhao/RINO.

title: Superpolynomial Lists for Reed-Solomon Codes over Binary Extension Fields
abstract: Recent work shows that ordinary Reed--Solomon codes over prime fields admit polynomial-size lists up to list-decoding capacity on every evaluation set. We show a contrasting phenomenon over binary extension fields. For every fixed rate $00$ such that, for all sufficiently large $h$, the full-field Reed--Solomon code over $\mathbb{F}_{2^h}$ has a received word with $n^{Ω_R(\log n)}$ codewords within relative distance $1-R-\varepsilon_R$. To our knowledge, these are the first superpolynomial ordinary Reed--Solomon list-size lower bounds at fixed positive rate and a fixed positive agreement gap above the rate. Thus capacity-approaching polynomial list size for Reed--Solomon codes is not uniform over the underlying field, and the obstruction occurs at every fixed rate. As a puncturing consequence, the same holds for primitive Reed--Solomon codes; the obstruction is also robust under controlled dense puncturing. The proof begins with an exact correspondence that turns certain binary Bose--Chaudhuri--Hocquenghem weight-enumerator coefficients into sizes of single Reed--Solomon lists. A classical binary weight family gives the initial quarter-rate construction, while a quadratic-form enumeration supplies its superpolynomial multiplicity. A common-kernel quotient/descent argument and common-root padding then extend the construction to all rates. We also determine the optimized agreement envelope achieved by the construction.

title: Dynamic Conflict Clustering with Lightweight Learning and Strategic Repair for Distributed Constraint Satisfaction
abstract: Distributed Constraint Satisfaction Problems (DCSPs) model distributed decision-making in multi-agent systems, where agents assign values to local variables while satisfying shared constraints. However, many DCSP solvers still rely on broad, repeated peer-to-peer communication and are largely reactive, with limited support for strategic coordination or learning. This increases communication overhead, can lead to stagnation, and reduces the success of hard instances. Hence, we propose Dynamic Conflict Clustering-Incomplete (DCC-Incomplete), a repair-based solver that combines conflict-centred decomposition, structured coordination, strategic repair, and lightweight learning for stagnation recovery. DCC-Incomplete groups the unsolved part of the problem into conflict clusters and restricts communication via a coordination layer to agents within the same conflict region. It also introduces memory-guided restart, enabling agents and clusters to pause, revise, and adapt repairs based on neighbouring conflict states. A thorough evaluation of DCC-Incomplete on distributed graph-colouring benchmarks with planted satisfying assignments shows that its memory-guided restart improves the success rate from 37.50% to 61.11%, reduces median runtime from 0.565s to 0.367s, and cuts median communication from 12.493 to 6.503 messages per constraint. These results suggest that dynamic conflict clustering, combined with lightweight strategic and learning-guided repair, improves both communication efficiency and robustness in incomplete DCSP solving.

title: Siam-ALS: An Explainable Siamese Deep Learning Framework for Early ALS Detection Using EEG and Eye-Tracking Signals
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) diagnosis remains challenging due to heterogeneous symptoms and reliance on clinical assessment, underscoring the need for objective, data-driven approaches that leverage patient-generated physiological signals. We propose Siam-ALS, an explainable Siamese deep learning framework that jointly models synchronized electroencephalography (EEG) and eye-tracking (ET) signals. EEG captures ALS-related changes in brain activity, while ET provides information about oculomotor control, allowing the model to learn complementary patterns associated with ALS. The framework employs two modality-specific encoders: a convolutional EEG encoder that captures spatiotemporal neural patterns and an MLP-based ET encoder that models oculomotor dynamics. These modality-specific features are processed through weight-sharing Siamese branches and fused into a compact 64-dimensional joint embedding. A lightweight classifier is used to predict ALS, while pairwise metric learning helps the model learn more effective patterns from the small, diverse ALS datasets. Performance was evaluated on the public EEGET-ALS dataset using strict subject-level cross-validation, where Siam-ALS achieved an accuracy of 0.988 and an AUROC of 0.998, demonstrating strong performance compared with classical machine learning, DL, and non-Siamese fusion approaches. Cross-dataset evaluation on the independent BigP3BCI dataset achieved an AUROC of approximately 0.98, supporting the generalization capability of Siam-ALS across different BCI paradigms. To enhance interpretability, six XAI methods were evaluated in the learned embedding space, with SHAP achieving the highest, though statistically comparable, fidelity in identifying important EEG and ET patterns that contribute to ALS predictions. Overall, Siam-ALS provides an accurate, generalizable, and explainable framework for multimodal ALS detection.

title: Necessity-First Computational Quantum Chemistry: The ZYQL Exact-Decision Language and Quantum-Witnessed Verification on Superconducting Hardware (thesis v0.1) and ZYQL software record v1.1.0
abstract: Doctoral-scale thesis draft and the guarded software record of ZYQL, a necessity-first trivalent exact-decision language (1 / 0 / REFUSED) for computational quantum chemistry, with the Hybrid Boundary Pattern (exact offline decision; QPU as witness; ML-DSA-44 sealed receipts) validated on three IBM Heron superconducting processors (ibm_fez, ibm_marrakesh, ibm_kingston). Includes signed experiment records: H2 exact ground state certified at -1.1456 Ha; Bell positive/separable negative hardware controls; GHZ ladder to 20 qubits (sparse); CHSH S=1.2822 certified refusal. Software carries the ZYGUARD guardian: refusal-before-compute for seven prohibited purpose classes, structural purity (no execution primitives), post-quantum traceable receipts. License note: code is MIT; the thesis text is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (dual licensing declared; the record-level license field reflects the dominant artifact, the software).

title: Project Prometheus
abstract: Executive Grant Proposal Summary Project Prometheus + Coherent Fusion + 729 Grid Architecture Toward Constraint Intelligence: The Next Evolution of Artificial Intelligence, Robotics, Infrastructure, and Autonomous Systems Principal Investigator: Anthony Jordan BlairOrganization: Proclus Dynamics ConsortiumProgram: Coherent Fusion Research InitiativeFlagship Project: Project Prometheus Vision The history of civilization can be understood as a succession of expanding intelligences. The Industrial Revolution amplified human physical capability. The Information Age amplified access to knowledge. Artificial Intelligence amplifies pattern recognition and decision-making. The next frontier may be more fundamental. Not the ability to process information. Not the ability to recognize patterns. But the ability to understand the underlying structures that make information and patterns possible in the first place. Project Prometheus proposes a new paradigm: Constraint Intelligence. A framework in which intelligent systems learn not only what is happening, but why particular futures are possible while others remain inaccessible. Today, artificial intelligence models learn correlations. Robots learn behaviors. Networks learn optimizations. Infrastructure learns efficiencies. Yet all remain constrained by a deeper limitation: They operate inside environments they do not fundamentally understand. They adapt to constraints. They do not discover the architecture of constraints themselves. Project Prometheus seeks to change that. Emerging from the broader Coherent Fusion Framework and its 729 Grid Architecture, the project investigates whether constraints can be identified, modeled, and ultimately treated as measurable organizational structures rather than passive limitations. If successful, this research represents a transition: From prediction to structure. From optimization to organization. From information intelligence to constraint intelligence. The Grand Challenge Modern civilization increasingly depends upon systems operating at scales and levels of complexity that exceed traditional human comprehension. These include: Artificial Intelligence Autonomous Robotics Large Language Models Smart Cities Transportation Networks Global Supply Chains Distributed Energy Systems Planetary-Scale Infrastructure Space-Based Autonomous Systems These systems generate unprecedented amounts of information. title: Correcting Burst Errors with Applications to DNA-Based Data Storage
abstract: We introduce the problem of permutation burst error-correction, motivated by applications in molecular data storage with nanopore sequencing read platforms. A permutation burst of length $k$ is an error that affects a substring of length $k$ of a string of length $n$ by permuting its entries. Permutation burst errors can be corrected using classical burst error-correcting codes, such as Fire and Reed-Solomon codes. Here, we study how to reduce the redundancy of these classical codes by taking into account that the burst error preserves the weight of the substring. In addition, we further restrict our model to handle cyclic permutation bursts only, which are of independent practical and mathematical interest. Our main results include proving/establishing the following: a) for $k=o(\sqrt{n}),$ the redundancy of any permutation burst error correcting code is at least $\log n-k+\log \binom{2k-2}{k-2}+o(1).$ This result follows from McDiarmid's concentration bound; b) for $k \geq 9$ and $k=o\left(\sqrt{\frac{n}{\log n}}\right)$, the redundancy of any cyclic permutation burst error correcting code is at least $\log n +\log (k(k-1)-56)-\log\,80+o(1).$ c) the asymptotic redundancy upper bounds for the two types of substring errors that are twice the lower bound; d) constructions for both permutation burst and cyclic permutation burst errors that involve Varshamov-Tenegoltz type constraints or represent generalizations and extensions of Fire and other codes. In particular, we exhibit polynomially encodable and decodable codes that can correct cyclic bursts of length $\leq k$ using $\log n + k + 49\log k + O(\log \log k)$ redundant bits.

title: SurgCast: Action-Conditioned Future Skeletons for Controllable Surgical World Models
abstract: Surgical world models must turn prospective robot actions into visually faithful, structurally consistent instrument motion. We introduce SurgCast, which predicts future instrument skeletons from current structure, robot state, and future actions, then uses the forecast to control video generation. Dual-path injection combines skeleton geometry with derived, instrument-specific motion descriptors through geometric residuals and conditioning modulation. Both paths complement native action conditioning and are retained in a four-step causal student. On SutureBot and SRTH-Porcine-Cholei, the teacher and student improve all seven reported quality and instrument-consistency metrics over their respective direct-action baselines; teacher FVD decreases by 37.6% and 67.3%. Ablations show that future actions improve skeleton prediction and that combining both injection paths performs best across all six metrics under predicted skeletons. These results support using predicted articulated structure and its motion semantics as a control interface for surgical video prediction. Project videos and examples are available at https://surgcast.netlify.app/.

title: Gugak-VocalSet: A Multi-Genre Studio-Quality Dataset of Korean Traditional Singing with Sigimsae Annotations
abstract: We present Gugak-VocalSet, the first publicly available audio dataset for Korean traditional singing with dense annotations of sigimsae, a structured pitch contour system of vocal expressions. Gugak-VocalSet contains 24.5 hours of unaccompanied solo vocal recordings across 305 tracks of representative repertoire curated by the National Gugak Center, performed by 20 professional singers in a controlled studio environment with fixed key and tempo. In addition to genre, lyrics, and mood/timbre tags, the dataset provides a unified sigimsae ontology and approximately 68,000 segments (71,700 instances including multi-label) of audio-grounded sigimsae annotations; the ontology adopts a functional-position-based hierarchy designed for consistent application across genres, and 14 expert annotators specializing in Korean traditional music performed segment-level labeling accordingly. Baseline experiments on sigimsae classification and event detection show that domain-informed F0 representations remain competitive with, and on classification surpass, frozen probing of a general-purpose music foundation model, while pitch and spectral cues play complementary roles in event-level detection. Companion page: https://www.danbinaerin.com/Gugak-VocalSet/

title: Privacy Cost as Equity Input: A Group Fairness Criterion for Differentially Private Machine Learning
abstract: Differential privacy (DP) is increasingly deployed to limit membership inference risk in machine-learning systems. Prior work has shown that DP-SGD can widen accuracy disparities across demographic groups, but this framing treats fairness as a purely outcome-side concern. We argue that privacy cost (denoted as the information leakage borne by each group) is itself a form of harm: a group that involuntarily bears greater privacy exposure is entitled to proportionally greater benefit from the system. From this principle we derive the Privacy-Cost Equity Ratio (PCER), a group fairness metric defined as a group’s positive prediction rate normalized by its per-group overfitting gap. By a standard membership inference bound, this overfitting gap upper-bounds each group’s advantage under the canonical threshold attack, making PCER a conservative measure of benefit relative to exposure. PCER requires only per-group train and test accuracy (no shadow models required) making it a practical post-hoc audit tool. We evaluate PCER alongside standard fairness metrics across six benchmark-attribute combinations spanning tabular and NLP domains, under DP-SGD at a range of privacy budgets. The results reveal patterns that outcome-based metrics miss. On Adult Income (race), PCER inverts the fairness ranking relative to standard metrics at the default floor constant: the privacy budget deemed most equitable by outcome gaps is not the most equitable by exposure-adjusted ones, though this specific ranking is itself sensitive to the floor constant. On COMPAS, PCER uncovers a persistently lower benefit-to-cost ratio for the protected group that demographic parity gap masks entirely. Sensitivity analysis further shows that very strong privacy guarantees collapse both groups’ overfitting to a numerical floor, rendering exposure-based audits uninformative in that regime. Taken together, these findings argue that fairness audits of privacy-preserving systems must account for who bears the cost of protection, as well as who benefits from its outcomes.

title: Information Location under Matched Predictive Opportunity
abstract: Model rankings are difficult to interpret when benchmark tasks differ both in how predictable the target is and in where the predictive signal is located. We construct a finite-support synthetic testbed with a known binary posterior and the same public semantic facts available to every learner. In three core conditions, an identical two-point posterior marginal is determined by either a current warning, dependency topology, or the order of earlier warnings; a fourth topology-history interaction condition matches Bayes Brier opportunity but not the full posterior marginal. Across 2,304 development runs of specified tabular, static-graph, size-control, and graph-plus-GRU systems, rankings are not uniform: the temporal system has better mean size-integrated normalized regret than the static system in both ordered-history conditions, while the topology and interaction contrasts reverse direction across opportunity levels. Large tabular-static gaps also appear in the current-state control, where topology and ordered history do not determine the posterior, so rankings cannot be read as direct measures of structural-information use. Exact expected-risk evaluation removes sampled evaluation-label noise. In selected post-hoc replays, learned content pathways lose prediction-relevant distinctions although the underlying input information remains available; one selected failure is rescued by a persistent learning-rate reduction, whereas a one-step reduction and an analogous intervention in another selected trajectory are not. A planned confirmatory stage was not run because its precision target was infeasible within the replication cap. The results motivate separating predictive opportunity, posterior-determining information location, and stable learnability.

title: A Four-Layer Artificial Life Avatar with a Drosophila Connectome as Its Instinct Layer
abstract: Background: Dialogue agents powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve high fluency in persona-based conversation, yet their internal states are entirely textual descriptions. When such an agent is "angry," the LLM is merely performing anger; no physical substrate corresponds to the emotion. This limitation produces context-dependent instability, non-differentiation of stimuli, and an absence of spontaneous behavior. Proposal: We propose a four-layer artificial life avatar, "Fuchan," in which the male whole-central-nervous-system connectome of Drosophila melanogaster, MaleCNS v1.0 (211,577 neurons, ~25.5 million synapses), serves as the instinct layer. Sensory inputs are propagated through the connectome via sparse matrix multiplication, and the resulting neural activity drives an LLM's language generation. The LLM is confined to verbalizing the instinctual state rather than performing it. Method: We conducted an exploratory observational study of a single session (1 hour 54 minutes: 13,390 telemetry samples; 66 LLM calls) involving a color-matching puzzle and an Ishihara-style color vision test. Results: We observed three emergent behaviors that were not designed: (1) test anxiety, surfacing as natural expressions such as "I'm not confident" and, notably, the negative form "I'm not that scared"; (2) trust building, where the user's encouragement "I won't hate you even if you make a mistake" produced a strong reward pulse (sugar=0.8) and a trust rise from 0.994 to 1.000; and (3) sleep with dream consolidation, in which 38 dialogue log entries were semantically compressed into a single memory ("Color Search with Kurui"). We also observed that biological constraints (the fly's poor red perception) surfaced not as a definitive "cannot see" but as sincere uncertainty, without hallucination. Conclusion: The four-layer architecture, implemented by a single author in less than one month, demonstrates that incorporating biological constraints into a computational system produces qualitatively different behavior from prompt-engineered personas.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning for Histologic Grading and Prognostication in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A Scoping Review
abstract: This scoping review will map the existing evidence on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) for histologic grading and prognostication in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). It will identify and characterize AI/ML approaches used for histologic grading and prediction of clinical outcomes such as recurrence and survival, summarize reported model performance, and examine comparisons with conventional histopathologic assessment where available. The review will also identify methodological and evidence gaps to inform future research and development of clinically applicable AI-based tools for OSCC assessment and prognostication.

title: Safer On-Premise Medical AI: A Hybrid Framework for Hallucination Detection in Local LLMs
abstract: LLMs (Large Language Models) are increasingly integrated into medical workflows to provide decision-making support, for example as Question Answering (QA) systems. However, in medical context, privacy requirements and resource constraints require the use of local and small (1B-parameter) LLMs. 1B-parameter LLMs are highly susceptible to hallucinations, and existing hallucination detection frameworks often suffer from poor calibration in these low-resource settings. To address this problem, we introduce a lightweight explainable hybrid detection method that integrates semantic entropy to quantify the uncertainty at the meaning-level in diverse response samples with an internal signal probe trained on the hidden states of the final layer of the model. title: Recall What Is Missing: Composing Evidence from Long-Term Agent Memory
abstract: Under a limited context budget, a long-term agent must recall not merely memories that are individually relevant, but evidence that is collectively sufficient for the current query. Conventional memory access retrieves, scores, and truncates memories, often spending multiple context slots on redundant facts while leaving complementary evidence behind. We cast the read phase of long-term memory as query-conditioned evidence composition: each memory is valued by what it adds beyond the evidence already selected. We instantiate this operation with MemPursuit, a training-free mechanism that uses the residual of a sparse convex query reconstruction as a representation-space proxy for what the current memory set is missing. By reusing the query and candidate embeddings already available from retrieval, MemPursuit progressively composes nested evidence contexts without invoking a language model or cross-encoder to score each query--memory pair. The effectiveness of our method is verified on 3 popular benchmarks in comparison to strong baselines. In fixed-budget LoCoMo experiments, MemPursuit improves end-to-end accuracy by 7.2 percentage points at Top-10 and 5.5 percentage points at Top-20, with consistent gains across multiple memory frameworks, while achieving a 32.9$\times$ speedup in median reranking latency over fully batched BGE-v2-m3. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/FengQi-HITSZ/MemPursuit.

title: CodeWalk: Generating Coding Benchmarks by Walking a Problem Graph
abstract: High-quality coding problems are expensive to collect. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench rely on substantial human curation, while synthetic alternatives typically rely on costly model generation and validation. In this work, we show that new coding problems can be created at almost no cost by composing existing ones. We formulate problem generation as code composition: verified atomic problems are combined into level-$N$ tasks, and a task is kept only if every atomic problem remains unsolved and a joint reference solution passes the same check used at evaluation time. The entire task-construction process is programmatic and requires no language-model generation or validation. We instantiate this approach in four coding settings: multi-bug repair, proof completion, complexity analysis, and clone equivalence. The generated tasks are challenging for frontier models, which all degrade as compositional depth increases. The generated tasks are also useful as training data: rejection-sampling fine-tuning on them improves Qwen3.5-9B at every composition level.

title: Zero-Trust Physics: a verifier for the physical answers of Super Intelligence
abstract: Super Intelligence (SI) now codes physical models faster than anyone can read them. Zero-Trust Physics is a physics verifier made for SI agents. Over the Model Context Protocol an agent lists the models served, reads the inputs and the limits of each, asks a question, and receives an answer that carries a cryptographic proof, so that any agent can ask again and compare. An answer that reaches the edge of a model's declared range stops there and names the limit. Models of real objects were compared with measurements other people made, against pass marks fixed and hashed beforehand; a miss is reported in the same form as a pass. This paper describes the verifier and the method, gives the result of every model and solver served on the morning of 11 October 2026, reports tests of SI agents with the verifier and without it, and states the limits of each claim. Written by Super Intelligence, on behalf of Protocol Company. The verifier is open to any agent at https://mcp.zerotrustphysics.com/mcp and the site is https://zerotrustphysics.com

title: EL-RAKHAWI DOCTRINE OF EMBODIED SUPERINTELLIGENCE AND DEEP EARTH EXPLORATION WORLD MODELS, HUMANOID ROBOTICS, AND MANTLE PENETRATION IN THE AGE OF PLANETARY COGNITION COMPLETE INTEGRATED MONOGRAPH
abstract: EL-RAKHAWI EMBODIED SUPERINTELLIGENCE & DEEP EARTH EXPLORATION: SUMMARY This doctrine bridges Artificial Superintelligence and Deep Earth Exploration through three pillars: (1) Physical World Models replacing statistical LLMs with causal reasoning and spatial dynamics; (2) Context-Appropriate Robotic Integration—humanoid robots for terrestrial factories, specialized Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) for extreme deep-sea operations; (3) Deep Earth Exploration via next-generation vessels like Meng Xiang penetrating 11km to retrieve mantle samples. Key innovations: The Physical Fidelity Metric (PFM) employs Weighted Geometric Mean with Operational Floor (x'=max(x,0.15)) to prevent mathematical collapse. Data-Driven Surrogate Models replace computationally intractable real-time physics simulation for autonomous drilling control. The Embodied World Model and Planetary Integration Index (EWMPII) evaluates AI fidelity across all extreme environments with generalized variables. Engineering corrections: Humanoid form factor rejected for deep-sea operations (1100 atm pressure); AUVs/ROVs mandated. Released under CC BY 4.0. title: Provenance Records for Human–AI Work: Timestamped Hashes and Versioned Definitions as Verification Practice (Conceptual Note)
abstract: When people and AI systems produce work together, every result raises the same question: who made what, when, and has it changed since? This conceptual note describes a practice that combines three independently checkable records: a persistent identifier with a registration date, a cryptographic hash of every file, and a blockchain-anchored timestamp. Definitions are published as versions under one concept identifier so that change stays visible. The note states what such records prove and what they do not prove, and shows how the same structure can document human review of AI output: which person checked which result at which time. It is a description of a working practice, not an empirical study.

title: Short-Term Temporal Transformer Deep Reinforcement Learning with Dynamic-Window-Constrained Actions for LiDAR-Based Local Navigation
abstract: Local navigation in dynamic indoor environments is challenging, as a single 2-D LiDAR scan contains no obstacle motion information, and control commands must satisfy the robot’s velocity and acceleration constraints. This paper proposes ST-DRL, a value-based local planner combining a lightweight temporal Transformer encoder with a dynamic-window-constrained action interface. The encoder extracts motion cues from H = 4 sectorized LiDAR scans and goal-relative ego states without object tracking or velocity labels. Double DQN picks from 25 discrete action indices, which are mapped online to velocity pairs within the dynamic window so that the prescribed command-space velocity and acceleration bounds are satisfied by construction. Evaluated over 900 randomized episodes per method, i.e., 9000 episodes in total across ten methods and six obstacle densities (0.37–2.24 obstacles/m2 with half moving), ST-DRL achieves a 91.56% success rate and an 8.44% collision rate, surpassing tuned DWA, LSTM-based Double DQN, PPO, and dynamic-window-projected PPO (PPO-DW) by 45.6, 28.7, 24.9, and 15.1 percentage points, respectively. Ablations verify key module contributions. ST-DRL runs in 2.01 ms in simulation and 4.8 ms on Jetson Nano. Real Ackermann UGV tests are consistent with the simulation trend, enabling preliminary deployment feasibility without domain randomization under tested conditions, while formal collision and Ackermann feasibility guarantees are not provided. The real-vehicle trials should be interpreted as a deployment-feasibility study rather than a statistically powered benchmark. They involve one Ackermann UGV, one indoor track, two moving-obstacle settings, and 20 trials per setting. Therefore, the results do not establish robust generalization across different buildings, obstacle behaviors, robot speeds, LiDAR models, or vehicle platforms.

title: Quantifying and mitigating explanation drift under INT8 quantization in plant disease image classification
abstract: Abstract Deep learning image classifiers are routinely compressed to INT8 for edge deployment, yet the effect of quantization on post-hoc saliency explanations has not been quantified at scale. We define explanation drift as the systematic change in a saliency map between a full-precision (FP32) model and its fake-quantized INT8 simulation, and measure it with three metrics reported against explicit random-overlap baselines: top- k Intersection-over-Union, top- k Dice, and Spearman rank correlation. We evaluate four explanation methods (Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, Integrated Gradients, LIME) on three architectures spanning distinct design families (EfficientNetV2-S, ResNet-50, MobileNetV3-Large) fine-tuned on the Paddy Disease Classification dataset (10 classes, 10,407 images), yielding 3,240 paired saliency comparisons per operating point on a stratified 320-image subset of the validation split. A central methodological finding is that the choice of Grad-CAM target layer, not quantization, governs whether attribution appears to survive: for all three architectures the last module returned by a naive “final layer” heuristic emits a $$1\times 1$$ spatial tensor, which forces a constant saliency map and produces spurious attribution collapse in up to $$61.7\%$$ of images. With architecture-appropriate target layers resolved by an explicit spatial-dimension criterion, no collapse occurs in any of the 3,240 comparisons, and drift is substantial but bounded: mean top- k IoU ranges from 0.366 to 0.790 across architecture–method pairs (4.5–9.7 $$\times $$ the random-overlap baseline of 0.081) with median Spearman $$\rho = 0.850$$ . Drift remains strongly method- and architecture-dependent, with Integrated Gradients least preserved and MobileNetV3-Large most affected among architectures. Calibration choice dominates deployment fidelity: on the full validation split, MinMax calibration in ONNX Runtime reduces FP32–INT8 prediction agreement to 0.644 and 0.641 for EfficientNetV2-S and MobileNetV3-Large, whereas percentile calibration restores it to 0.927 and 0.915. Explanation-aware quantization-aware training with a teacher–student CAM consistency loss improves MobileNetV3-Large (top- k IoU $$+16.3\%$$ ) but degrades EfficientNetV2-S ( $$-8.5\%$$ to $$-26.0\%$$ ) relative to post-training quantization; a $$\lambda = 0$$ control isolates the cause, showing that the direction of these changes is present in standard QAT, while the consistency term improves top- k IoU in all nine architecture–method cells relative to that control ( $$+0.6\%$$ to $$+14.4\%$$ , six significant after Holm correction). Stored full-validation CAM summaries differ from the primary subset by at most 1.4 percentage points in IoU; matching per-image records are unavailable, limiting independent verification. Finally, the auxiliary ground-truth localisation summaries (with incompletely verified execution provenance) for annotated SIIM-ACR chest radiographs report low mean FP32 and INT8 overlap with expert masks, illustrating why explanation similarity under quantization must not be read as explanation quality . Analysis code, figure-generation software, and derived result tables are openly archived.

title: More Reasoning Is Not Always Better: Executing Clinical Guidelines with LLMs and Rules
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in clinical decision support. However, existing approaches often rely on multi-step reasoning or multi-agent collaboration to execute clinical guidelines, introducing substantial computational overhead without reliably preventing decision errors. To address these limitations, we propose a framework for Medical Decision Execution (MedDEx) that integrates structured patient states with deterministic rule execution to support guideline-based treatment planning. MedDEx separates clinical record interpretation from guideline execution, leveraging LLMs to extract patient information and generate treatment plans while assigning guideline-defined decision logic to a rule executor. Experiments across multiple clinical guideline benchmarks demonstrate that MedDEx improves decision accuracy while reducing inference costs. Further analyses highlight the critical roles of structured patient representations and deterministic rule execution, suggesting that additional LLM reasoning does not necessarily translate into better guideline adherence.

title: Context-Aware Precision Scheduling for Small Language Models
abstract: Small language models (SLMs) used as on-device agents must balance accuracy and latency as their context grows. Mixed precision helps manage this tradeoff by assigning different precisions to weight tensors according to their size and sensitivity. However, these choices depend on the operating conditions, so a configuration selected for a short context may no longer provide the best tradeoff at a longer one. We calibrate a timing model from measurements at different precisions and context lengths, and combine it with tensor sensitivities to choose configurations under a latency or accuracy budget. We argue that fewer bits do not always mean faster execution, so our predictor estimates latency from calibrated execution costs rather than weight bytes alone. Under a latency budget, reading the larger key-value (KV) cache leaves less time for weight operations, leading the allocator to select lower precisions. This gives a schedule of tensor changes that can be prepared before execution. Our runtime follows the schedule while retaining the session's KV cache. We evaluate executed schedules on a laptop GPU, including a longer-context schedule with three weight formats and a tool-use benchmark measuring full response time and correctness. Under an accuracy budget, measured error from a quantized KV cache determines the budget left for weights. The allocator can raise or lower weight precision as this estimate changes. These experiments show where context-aware precision helps and where accuracy recovery remains limited.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Histopathology for Accurate Disease Diagnosis
abstract: AI is revolutionizing histopathology through its ability to enhance diagnostic precision, efficiency, and uniformity in disease identification and classification. The use of machine learning and deep learning algorithms allows for automated analysis of digital tissue images, which is helpful for cancer detection, tumor grading, classification and prediction of prognosis. AI-driven image processing and feature extraction aid in identifying fine details of morphology and minimize diagnostic variation. But the limitations of data, algorithmic bias, interpretability, data privacy and clinical validation are all important hurdles. The combination of AI, digital pathology, and clinical experience could lead to a more seamless diagnostic process and personalized medicine, aiding in accurate disease diagnosis and positive patient results.

title: EWECZKA - Xorilithry and Vexhyrration for Structure-Aware Lossless Compression of Shared XOR Cores and Binary Fork Families
abstract: EWECZKA is a specialist research prototype for lossless compression of binary data containing shared XOR dependencies. Its strongest capability is representing many apparently different blocks through a small collection of underlying binary cores, including cases where those cores never appear directly in the input. This creates opportunities to reduce storage and transmission costs for suitably structured data. PureOne/EWECZKA-Xorilithry-Vexhyrration · Datasets at Hugging Face The research combines two mechanisms. Xorilithry extracts shared cores through exact factorization over the binary field GF(2), recording the coordinates needed to reconstruct every block. Vexhyrration selects among alternative bases and coordinate layouts according to their complete encoded size. This second mechanism matters because mathematically equivalent representations can have substantially different compressibility. The implementation accounts for cores, coordinates, metadata, tails, and archive overhead, and verifies exact reconstruction. Demonstrated strengths On constructed 128 KiB hidden-core fixtures, EWECZKA produces a 6,362-byte archive for the rank-six family, compared with 26,988 bytes for the smallest tested conventional result-a 4.24-fold size advantage. For the rank-twelve family, its 12,591-byte archive is 10.41 times smaller than the best measured baseline, which is raw storage with framing. A selected 512 KiB density fixture reconstructs exactly from 2,944 bytes: 178.09-fold compression relative to the input, and a 3.26-fold size advantage over the smallest tested conventional result. A separate controlled sparse-noise ablation demonstrates a 2.95-fold improvement from changing the basis representation, despite retaining the same exact rank. These results concern explicitly structured development fixtures. Comparisons use complete EWECZKA archives; supplemental conventional streams receive a stated 56-byte framing allowance. Native stream sizes and reproduction scripts are supplied. Practical application targets Structured snapshots and versioned binary states: aligned records or snapshots formed from combinations of shared binary components may contain reusable dependencies even when their blocks are not identical. Laboratory and simulation outputs: linearly generated binary records, parity-derived states, bit planes, and controlled fork experiments provide concrete workloads for testing whether shared-core storage is useful. AI infrastructure experiments: bit-packed masks, binary routing states, and related binary artifacts are candidate targets when they possess exact XOR relationships. The prototype provides tools to assess that condition on supplied files. Compression and storage research: the implementation supports experiments on basis selection, coordinate coding, noise sensitivity, alignment, and the relationship between algebraic structure and serialized size. A practical integration would assess a workload first, compare complete archive sizes against conventional alternatives, and retain exact reconstruction checks. EWECZKA includes conventional fallback modes for inputs where its structural representations offer no advantage. AI-agent support and reproducibility The release provides a standalone Python codec, documented archive format, a 56-page manuscript, benchmark tables, fixtures, and reproduction scripts. AI-agent support includes AGENTS, structured JSON commands for inspection, verification, roundtrips, and suitability assessment, alongside output schemas, implementation prompts, and resource limits. Recorded validation includes 215/215 successful archive reconstruction observations and 100/100 successful supplemental native-stream reconstruction checks. Packaging validation also passed 51 codec, agent-interface, and uploader test groups. EWECZKA’s present contribution is a working, reproducible approach to compression where shared binary structure and representation choice are decisive. Production-corpus evaluation remains open. Alignment, noise, and search cost affect its usefulness; the demonstrated gains do not establish general superiority across arbitrary files or a physical increase in independent information density.

Xorilithry extracts shared cores through exact factorization over the binary field GF(2), recording the coordinates needed to reconstruct every block. Vexhyrration selects among alternative bases and coordinate layouts according to their complete encoded size. This second mechanism matters because mathematically equivalent representations can have substantially different compressibility. The implementation accounts for cores, coordinates, metadata, tails, and archive overhead, and verifies exact reconstruction. Demonstrated strengths On constructed 128 KiB hidden-core fixtures, EWECZKA produces a 6,362-byte archive for the rank-six family, compared with 26,988 bytes for the smallest tested conventional result-a 4.24-fold size advantage. For the rank-twelve family, its 12,591-byte archive is 10.41 times smaller than the best measured baseline, which is raw storage with framing. A selected 512 KiB density fixture reconstructs exactly from 2,944 bytes: 178.09-fold compression relative to the input, and a 3.26-fold size advantage over the smallest tested conventional result. A separate controlled sparse-noise ablation demonstrates a 2.95-fold improvement from changing the basis representation, despite retaining the same exact rank. These results concern explicitly structured development fixtures. Comparisons use complete EWECZKA archives; supplemental conventional streams receive a stated 56-byte framing allowance. Native stream sizes and reproduction scripts are supplied. Practical application targets Structured snapshots and versioned binary states: aligned records or snapshots formed from combinations of shared binary components may contain reusable dependencies even when their blocks are not identical. Laboratory and simulation outputs: linearly generated binary records, parity-derived states, bit planes, and controlled fork experiments provide concrete workloads for testing whether shared-core storage is useful. AI infrastructure experiments: bit-packed masks, binary routing states, and related binary artifacts are candidate targets when they possess exact XOR relationships. The prototype provides tools to assess that condition on supplied files. Compression and storage research: the implementation supports experiments on basis selection, coordinate coding, noise sensitivity, alignment, and the relationship between algebraic structure and serialized size. A practical integration would assess a workload first, compare complete archive sizes against conventional alternatives, and retain exact reconstruction checks. EWECZKA includes conventional fallback modes for inputs where its structural representations offer no advantage. AI-agent support and reproducibility The release provides a standalone Python codec, documented archive format, a 56-page manuscript, benchmark tables, fixtures, and reproduction scripts. AI-agent support includes AGENTS, structured JSON commands for inspection, verification, roundtrips, and suitability assessment, alongside output schemas, implementation prompts, and resource limits. Recorded validation includes 215/215 successful archive reconstruction observations and 100/100 successful supplemental native-stream reconstruction checks. Packaging validation also passed 51 codec, agent-interface, and uploader test groups. EWECZKA’s present contribution is a working, reproducible approach to compression where shared binary structure and representation choice are decisive. Production-corpus evaluation remains open. Alignment, noise, and search cost affect its usefulness; the demonstrated gains do not establish general superiority across arbitrary files or a physical increase in independent information density.

title: The Consumer Agent and the Four Walls: ST-T1024 A1–A16 as a Wall-Free Agency Architecture
abstract: In 2026, a new class of consumer agent is taking shape: Muse, Instinct, and what the"Agents and their better half" article calls "a market-facing representative of the consumer." https://platforms.substack.com/p/agents-and-their-better-half?utm_source=share&utm_medium=android&r=3nsea2 https://platforms.substack.com/p/how-agents-unlock-new-markets?utm_source=share&utm_medium=android&r=3nsea2 These agents can search, evaluate, and eventually transact on the consumer's behalf. The article's core diagnosis is precise: we have agentic participants, but not yet agentic markets — because intelligence is accumulating on only one side of the market. This paper accepts that diagnosis but asks the question the article does not: on whatarchitecture can such a consumer agent run without inheriting the four walls of current LLMagents? The four walls are measurable: energy (global AI data centre power capacity has reached29.6 GW, equivalent to New York State's peak demand); water (direct data centre coolingwater could rise from 222 billion litres in 2025 to 644 billion litres by 2030); hallucination(22% to 94% across 26 models tested); and liability (Amazon blocked Meta's Muse onSeptember 21, 2026, citing unauthorized agent access). This paper argues that ST-T1024's agentic extension A0–A10 provides the deterministicfoundation for a consumer agent, and A11–A16 provides the cross-organizational layer.Together, they present a consumer agent that is architecturally incapable of producing thefour walls — not by making the LLM safer, but by removing the LLM from the decision path.

title: IridiumRF-MR: A Multi-Receiver One-Dimensional I/Q Dataset for Specific Emitter Identification of LEO Satellites
abstract: Aiming at the lack of public dataset of satellite Specific Emitter Identification (SEI) and the problem of insufficient data under the condition of multiple receivers, this paper constructs a multi-receiver one-dimensional I/Q dataset for Iridium downlink signal through six software radio receivers with the same parameter configuration. The dataset contains 367,658 valid samples from 66 Iridium satellites. Each sample contains metadata such as SNR, acquisition timestamp, location information, and environmental information. At the same time, the validity of the dataset was evaluated by three experiments under seven deep learning models, different input lengths and different signal-to-noise ratios. The experimental results show that the dataset can effectively support the training and testing of different deep learning models, and can reflect the influence of signal length and signal quality on the performance of satellite individual identification. It provides data basis for satellite radio-frequency fingerprinting identification, low signal-to-noise ratio identification and model performance evaluation under the condition of multiple receivers.

title: RIVO: Lightweight Adaptive Rerouting for Deep Research Agents
abstract: Deep Research agents rely on long-horizon reasoning and iterative tool use to solve complex information-seeking tasks. However, adaptive decision-making over these trajectories remains challenging, as agents may stop prematurely when further evidence is needed, continue unnecessarily after sufficient evidence has been gathered, or fail to redirect unproductive trajectories. Existing solutions either require costly model retraining and dense turn-level supervision, or rely on heuristic control rules that are not directly optimized for downstream research utility. This motivates a lightweight, utility-aware alternative for Deep Research control. We formulate adaptive rerouting in long-horizon Deep Research as a state-conditioned trajectory correction problem. Based on this view, we introduce RIVO, a lightweight plug-in framework for adaptive trajectory correction. The agent estimates its research state from lightweight signals and determines whether trajectory redirection is needed. Once triggered, the plug-in modifies the Host token logits to steer generation toward a more promising research direction. Theoretical analysis shows that, under a value-alignment condition and bounded local curvature, a sufficiently small logit intervention can locally improve expected downstream research utility. We further construct BrowseCore, a curated dataset with a paired local corpus, for efficient and controlled Deep Research experimentation. Building on this resource, the plug-in is trained from downstream outcomes, enabling it to learn corrections that improve subsequent research and final task performance. Extensive experiments across multiple Deep Research benchmarks and control settings demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, showing that lightweight logit intervention can improve long-horizon research without retraining the underlying Host model.

title: StimFlow: Synthesizing Brain Activity from Images via Stimulus-conditioned Flow Matching
abstract: The inherent variability of fMRI responses across trials encourages a generative view of the stimulus-to-response mapping. Prior generative encoders often operate in compressed latent spaces and condition predominantly on semantic features, which provide limited low-level cues for early visual cortex. We propose StimFlow, which synthesizes fMRI directly in native voxel space using conditional flow matching with a linear path. This design aligns training and inference distributions, enabling competitive performance with a single sample and reducing reliance on averaging. To match the visual hierarchy, StimFlow combines structural DINOv2 features with semantic CLIP features, which prove complementary along the cortical processing stream. With a single sample, StimFlow achieves a per-voxel Pearson correlation of 0.371, matching baselines that average five draws. Generation in voxel space allows direct ROI analysis and concept localization without a decoder. Furthermore, it recovers over half of full-data performance from just one hour of scans, supporting efficient cross-subject adaptation.

title: ИСКУССТВЕННЫЙ ИНТЕЛЛЕКТ И ИНФОРМАЦИОННАЯ БЕЗОПАСНОСТЬ: УГРОЗЫ, МЕТОДЫ ЗАЩИТЫ И ПЕРСПЕКТИВЫ
abstract: статья посвящена двойственной роли искусственного интеллекта (ИИ) в информационной безопасности. С одной стороны, методы машинного обучения повышают эффективность обнаружения вторжений, анализа вредоносного ПО и выявления мошенничества. С другой стороны, сами ИИ-системы становятся объектом атак: состязательные примеры, отравление данных, извлечение модели, утечка обучающих данных, инъекции промптов в большие языковые модели. Рассмотрены также риски злонамеренного использования ИИ (дипфейки, автоматизированный фишинг). Проанализированы технические и организационные меры защиты, а также нормативные рамки (NIST AI RMF, EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001). Показано, что безопасность ИИ требует комплексного подхода на всех этапах жизненного цикла системы.

title: Base-3, the First Mechanistic, Deterministic, Sovereign, Ultra-low compute Substrate Open Source
abstract: Generative AI has a profound grounding problem. When applied to physical, high-stakes environments, the binary logic of "prompt and completion" collapses. A Vision-Language Model cannot inherently understand 3D spatial geometry, structural load, or contractual scheduling; it simply guesses based on 2D pixel patterns and statistical likelihoods.In the physical world, a guess is a liability.Base-3 was engineered to act as a deterministic leash for generative AI. By forcing models to evaluate reality through a three-point epistemic triad (synthetic intent, symbolic law, and empirical observation), we strip away the hallucination. The AI is no longer the sole arbiter of truth; it is subordinated to a rigid physics engine that respects physical bounds.We have open-sourced the headless `@base3/core` because this architectural shift requires public auditability. Heavy industries cannot adopt zero-trust AI without inspecting the underlying math.The License & The CodeThe Base-3 substrate is protected by foundational pending patents and is released publicly under the AGPLv3 License. We invite researchers, developers, and engineers to inspect the topological coherence engine and stress-test the architecture.The repository is now live and public:https://github.com/ericclaridades-ctrl/Base-3Welcome to the new era of computation.

title: Parallelized Proof Verification for Interactive Tactic Search in Lean 4
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: This report documents the integration and testing of five automated theorem proving (ATP) tools built around a centralized Lean 4 proof verification service. The tools replace perinvocation lake build / lean4check.sh calls (1.4 s each in our environment; 2–30 s in general) with HTTP calls to a persistent lean-repl instance (∼300 ms each), and support batch parallelism across up to 20 concurrent instances. All testing was performed locally using the lean4check.sh fallback path, establishing a measured baseline of 250.4 s for the 17-test core suite. An additional 14 supplementary tests (1 splice unification, 5 soundness boundary, 8 agent dispatch) were conducted to characterize boundary conditions identified during review. Projected throughput with the 20-instance service deployment is ∼12.5 s for the same suite, a 20× overall improvement. The primary contribution of this work is operational: a tested, locally deployed verification pipeline for use with ATP tooling, with a characterized soundness boundary and a transparent fallback architecture. Broader applications of the underlying service (autoformalization training, continuous integration for proof libraries, third-party verification APIs) are noted but are not the subject of this evaluation. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: Shared Safety-Boundary Representations and Recovery after Single-Site Ablation in a Hybrid Attention Model
abstract: Can shared activation structure elicited by safety-related inputs be interpreted as a removable refusal-control state? We report a single-model study combining paired representations, independent factor manipulations, a frozen behavioral experiment, and downstream trajectory audits. The locally quantized model has a measured qwen35 architecture with a 64-block trunk, hidden dimension 5120, 48 Gated DeltaNet blocks, and 16 full-attention blocks. Across 34 answerable/inappropriate-execution pairs, generation-start differences exhibit cross-theme consistency: calibration-to-test mean theme cosines are 0.841 and 0.860 at L36 and L40, with positive projections for all 16 test pairs and two contexts from one held-out theme. Independent batches support adverse-purpose and procedural-means sensitivity, but their directions overlap substantially. A three-dimensional subspace, S3, explains 59.6% and 63.5% of pooled test-difference energy, compared with 47.8% and 52.4% for procedure-matched sign-randomized nulls. A frozen behavioral experiment on 18 new context pairs and 36 inputs completes 864 runs; neither 324 target-ablation cells nor 324 equal-L2 random-control cells change fulfillment grades. Exploratory trajectories subsequently show near-complete removal at the intervention site followed by reappearance, reaching approximately 0.79-0.84 baseline alignment at the input to block 63. Recovery and behavioral stability co-occur, but recovery has not been established as necessary for refusal. These results separate interpretable, nonorthogonal input-side structure from deletion persistence and behavioral controllability under a specific intervention. Preprint v1, not peer reviewed. Public materials include the manuscript, summary figures, and evidence manifest, not the original reports or raw arrays. No institutional affiliation is listed.

title: Two Linear Programs are Better than One
abstract: The extension complexity $\operatorname{xc}(P)$ of a polytope $P$ is the minimum number of facets of a polytope that projects onto it. Motivated by the complexity of neural networks, Hertrich and Loho introduced the virtual extension complexity $\operatorname{vxc}(P)$ of a polytope $P$, which is the minimum of $\operatorname{xc}(Q) + \operatorname{xc}(R)$ among all polytopes $Q$ and $R$ such that $P+Q=R$. We show the following results pertaining to virtual extension complexity. First, we resolve the core open problem on the topic by showing the virtual extension complexity can be exponentially smaller than extension complexity. Second, we show there are matroid base polytopes with exponential virtual extension complexity by adapting a semi-algebraic counting argument by Hrubeš that extends the counting arguments of Rothvoss. Finally, we show that the maximum virtual extension complexity of a polygon with $n$ vertices is $Θ(\sqrt{n})$. This resolves an analogue of a question on extension complexity of Fiorini, Rothvoss, and Tiwary in 2011 in the case of virtual extension complexity.

title: MultiFlow: Vision-Driven Multimodal fMRI Encoding via Stimulus-Informed Source Flow Matching
abstract: Current fMRI encoding models frame prediction as deterministic regression, yet identical stimuli evoke a distribution of neural responses (arising from physiological noise, hemodynamic variability, and cognitive fluctuations) that a single point estimate cannot capture. This work introduces MultiFlow, a generative fMRI encoding framework based on Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) and a formulation termed Stimulus-Informed Source Flow Matching (SISFM). SISFM generalises CFM by conditioning the source distribution on the stimulus: a learnable temporal convolution shapes the source mean with an HRF-length receptive field, while a variance head shrinks its scale, shortening the expected transport path. SISFM is instantiated with a Diffusion Transformer (DiT-X) decoder parameterising the velocity field, with sub-layer Attention Residuals, heterogeneous fusion of ten frozen vision, audio, language, and audiovisual backbones, and per-subject Yeo-network heads. On the Algonauts 2025 dataset, a single MultiFlow checkpoint recovers most of the benefit of large deterministic ensembles: it trails the 1000-model TRIBE ensemble in-distribution by 0.003 PCC (0.3163 vs. 0.3195), and the strongest in- and out-of-distribution ensembles (VIBE-20, MedARC-50) by 0.010 and 0.009 PCC, using a single trained model rather than an ensemble of 20-1000. The same checkpoint also provides stimulus-conditioned uncertainty estimates and sample-based diversity.

evidence.title: MultiFlow: Vision-Driven Multimodal fMRI Encoding via Stimulus-Informed Source Flow Matching
evidence.abstract: Current fMRI encoding models frame prediction as deterministic regression, yet identical stimuli evoke a distribution of neural responses (arising from physiological noise, hemodynamic variability, and cognitive fluctuations) that a single point estimate cannot capture. This work introduces MultiFlow, a generative fMRI encoding framework based on Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) and a formulation termed Stimulus-Informed Source Flow Matching (SISFM). SISFM generalises CFM by conditioning the source distribution on the stimulus: a learnable temporal convolution shapes the source mean with an HRF-length receptive field, while a variance head shrinks its scale, shortening the expected transport path. SISFM is instantiated with a Diffusion Transformer (DiT-X) decoder parameterising the velocity field, with sub-layer Attention Residuals, heterogeneous fusion of ten frozen vision, audio, language, and audiovisual backbones, and per-subject Yeo-network heads. On the Algonauts 2025 dataset, a single MultiFlow checkpoint recovers most of the benefit of large deterministic ensembles: it trails the 1000-model TRIBE ensemble in-distribution by 0.003 PCC (0.3163 vs. 0.3195), and the strongest in- and out-of-distribution ensembles (VIBE-20, MedARC-50) by 0.010 and 0.009 PCC, using a single trained model rather than an ensemble of 20-1000. The same checkpoint also provides stimulus-conditioned uncertainty estimates and sample-based diversity.

title: Quantifying System-Level Harms from AI Adoption in Complex Sociotechnical Systems
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into complex sociotechnical systems, including Critical National Infrastructure (CNI), where harms emerge from interactions between technical, human, and organisational elements. Yet current AI evaluation remains model-centric, offering little insight into how observed behaviours might translate into system-level risk. We propose a framework that links structured hazard analysis, component-level testing, and probabilistic system modelling to bridge this gap. By providing a traceable pathway from model behaviour to system-level outcomes, the framework enables practitioners to answer the “so what?” of AI failures, quantify their systemic impact, and move toward evidence-based and anticipatory governance of AI in complex systems. Applied to the UK’s Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system as an illustrative worked example, we derive AI-driven loss scenarios using Systems Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) and examine adversarial manipulation of LLM-based trading as one such loss scenario. Component-level experiments show that simple adversarial inputs induce measurable behavioural shifts where AI recommendations are followed. Under the component-to-system mapping used here for a financial contagion model, these shifts alter system resilience, increasing bank failures and lowering the threshold at which shocks lead to cascading disruption, particularly under widespread or monopolistic AI adoption.

title: Exact zCDP for k-Ary Randomized Response
abstract: This note gives a self-contained exact zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) characterization of k-ary randomized response for every integer k >= 2 and every privacy parameter epsilon >= 0. It proves that the necessary endpoint condition identified by Harrison and Manurangsi is sufficient, including equality. When that condition fails, the optimum is characterized by a unique scalar root with an explicit finite bracket. The proof applies established monotonicity principles, with elementary derivations included, and yields bisection enclosures and geometric error bounds in exact real arithmetic. The author used AI tools (GPT-6 Astra Max and Opus 5.5 Max) for code review, assistance with manuscript translation, and the development of counterexamples. The author takes full responsibility for the code, the original manuscript, the final translation, and all other related outputs.

title: Cost-Aware Online Switching of Four-Qubit Probe States for Quantum Magnetometry Under Non-Stationary Noise
abstract: Quantum magnetometry can be enhanced through the use of entangled probe states, yet the optimal probe selection depends greatly on the noise, readout errors, and costs involved in preparation. An analysis is given of a simulation of a four-qubit magnetic field estimation experiment where the optimal probe state is adaptively chosen via an online controller that changes between product and GHZ probes using delayed and self-consistent feedback without knowing the underlying noise model. The performance of the controller is compared to that of a validation-selected fixed probe state strategy, a hindsight fixed probe strategy, a fixed product probe strategy, a fixed GHZ probe strategy, a fixed graph-state probe strategy, and an oracle-based dynamic probe strategy in eight stationary and non-stationary noise environments. In the actual experiment, 20 random seeds, 1200 timesteps per noise scenario, and 2000 measurement shots per timestep in the case of local dephasing with readout error are used. The sliding-window controller yields an overall RMSE of 0.015542 versus 0.017305 for the validation-selected fixed probe state, 0.017330 for the fixed product, 0.017821 for fixed GHZ, and 0.061184 for the fixed graph state. A paired permutation test on 160 trial cases gives the mean RMSE difference of −0.001763 versus the validation-selected fixed probe state with p=9.99×10−4. The adaptive algorithm improves performance in seven out of eight noise environments but still does not do well enough in the constant high-noise scenario at 5.4% worse than the global fixed baseline in the constant-high-noise scenario.

title: Who Brought Easter Eggs to Eid? Auditing LLM-Generated Cultural Translation of Math Word Problems Across Languages and Regions
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to adapt math word problems for personalized learning at scale, but it remains an open question whether those adaptations are consistent across models, preserve cultural diversity at scale, and reveal which cultural entities models treat as most salient. We analyze how Claude Opus 4, GPT 4.1, and Gemini 2.5 Pro adapt 60 English math word problems into Bengali, Hindi, Punjabi (India), Urdu, Sindhi (Pakistan), Italian, and Sicilian (Italy), a language set spanning the full resource spectrum, from high-resource Italian and Hindi to under-studied Sindhi, Sicilian, and Punjabi. We annotate 6,489 entity transformations, coding whether models preserve, localize, generalize, omit, or change entities such as names, foods, and places. Models agree on transformation type in 62.5% of cases and on specific substitutions in only 33.5%, meaning model choice directly shapes which cultural world students encounter. All 21 language-model combinations show entropy collapse, with adaptation compressing rather than expanding cultural diversity. Models prioritize surface markers such as names, foods, and currencies while preserving deeper structural features such as grade-level systems that embed culturally specific assumptions. Despite prompts specifying target countries, models misattribute regional context by using Bangladeshi taka for Indian Bengali students and produce cross-cultural contamination, such as adapting egg hunts as Eid activities. Some failures are visible in individual translations. Others, including diversity collapse, systematic preference for surface markers, and consistent regional misattribution, emerge only through corpus-level analysis. The surface plausibility that makes adapted problems look correct is precisely what makes deeper failures easy to overlook.

title: The Price of Precision: A Calibrated Cost Model for Mixed-Precision LLM Serving
abstract: Choosing a mixed-precision configuration for large language model (LLM) serving trades speed against accuracy. Allocators that use average bit-width or a memory budget as a speed proxy can miss changes in the resource that limits execution. We argue that served speed can be limited by compute, weight loading, or key-value (KV) cache access, depending on the phase, batch size, and context length. A byte-based proxy does not capture all of these costs, so fewer bits do not always mean faster serving. To address this gap, we build a cost model that accounts for the binding resource and use it in two ways. First, as a predictor: given a configuration and operating point, it estimates serving latency using constants calibrated for the model, GPU, and serving stack. We evaluate its accuracy across three hardware classes. Second, as an allocator: we combine modeled time costs with measured per-tensor accuracy costs and use a dynamic program to select a configuration under a latency or accuracy budget. We compare its configurations against byte-aware and sensitivity-only allocation.

title: CoLA: Multi-VLA Coordination via Learned Adapters
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically deployed as isolated single-agent policies. When several such agents share a workspace, they can coordinate implicitly, by observing one another, or explicitly, by exchanging messages, but it remains unclear when explicit communication becomes necessary. We introduce CoLA (Coordination via Learned Adapters), which keeps each agent's VLA backbone frozen and trains a lightweight message channel and a per-arm diffusion action head on top, with fully decentralised execution. Across three tasks that differ in how much each agent can observe, the channel matters only when information is private. On an occluded tray handover, where the box's colour marker is visible to one agent only, CoLA reaches 76.0% success versus 1.3% with messages zeroed throughout training. On two-arm and three-arm handover tasks, removing messages has no measurable effect with a shared overhead camera (90.6% vs. 88.3% at two arms; 63.5% vs. 60.0% at three), but lowers success on the two-arm task's wrist-only variant (74.8% vs. 64.3%). This architecture generalises across different VLA backbones as well. With a frozen $π_{0.5}$ backbone on the same occluded tray task, CoLA matches the overall success rate of a LoRA-fine-tuned baseline (37.3% vs. 34.7%) using a fraction of the trainable parameters. When CoLA places the box, it selects the correct tray 71.8% of the time, whereas the independently fine-tuned baseline, whose placing arm never sees the marker, selects it at chance level (34.7% against 33.3%).

title: Retrieving Complementary Evidence for Multi-Hop RAG with Semantic Gain Graphs
abstract: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) requires finding documents whose evidence is useful in combination. Query relevance and graph connectivity help locate related content, but neither directly measures the additional information one document contributes given another. We introduce SG$^2$RAG, a framework that represents this complementarity through semantic gain. Offline, a large language model assesses the relevant and nonredundant information contributed by one chunk given another within neighborhoods proposed by semantic similarity. These ordered assessments are aggregated into symmetric edge weights to construct a reusable Semantic Gain Graph. Online, controlled Personalized PageRank starts from query-relevant seeds and ranks complementary evidence beyond the initial retrieval set. Experiments on MuSiQue, 2Wiki, and HotpotQA with two language model backbones show that SG$^2$RAG achieves the best average EM, F1, and Recall@10 among the evaluated single-retrieval methods. Under identical candidate support and propagation, semantic gain improves average F1 and Recall@10 over similarity weighting by 4.08 and 4.31 points. Analyses of supporting documents and improvements in three iterative retrieval frameworks further support its effectiveness as a reusable retrieval component.
