title: Data from Radiometer (RAD) measurements at Paris – Nangis (PANANG) from 2023-01-26 to 2024-03-27 [L0]
abstract: Combined and unfiltered logger data from radiometer measurements of global shortwave irradiance and longwave irradiance at Nangis (Départment 77) in the rural area to the SE of Greater Paris recorded during the urbisphere Paris Campaign from 2023-01-26 00:00 to 2024-03-27 00:00 UTC. Measurements were taken at the MétéoFrance weather station at Nangis on the airfield at Nangis-les-Loges LFAI (ID 77211001) at 48.595124°N / 3.007791°E. Radiometer measurements taken at PANANG are: Global (solar) hemispherical irradiance (GHI) with an intermittently ventilated Kipp&Zonen CM21 pyranometer Longwave hemispherical irradiance (LHI) with an intermittently ventilated and Kipp&Zonen CG1 or CG4 pyrgeometer (from 2023-01-26 18:00:00 to 2023-03-22 15:00:00 a CG4 pyrgeometer was operated, from 2023-03-22 15:15:00 to 2024-03-27 13:04:00 a CG1 pyrgeometer was operated). The values in this dataset are calibrated using manufacturer calibrations for all instruments and no further quality controlls or gap filling procedures have been applied. For quality controlled and calibrated data use L1 data and higher instead. The two L0 datafiles (RAW_1min, MET_1min) combine all individual (uncalibrated voltage and manufacturer calibrated) logger files (automatic transfer, manual download) with a consistent and consecutive time axis. Missing data is filled with -9999. Each data file is structured with time steps as rows and parameters as column in comma-separated csv format. The columns contain readings from two radiometers and a co-located T/RH sensor (Campbell Scientific HygroVue 10) and Surface brightness temperature measured (Campbell Scientific IR120 IRT Thermometer) pointing to the grass surface. Files have 4 header lines following the Campbell Scientific Inc. TOA5 file definition. title: DentDeID: open, tested de-identification for dental images
abstract: DentDeID removes patient-identifying information from dental images: DICOM attributes following the DICOM PS3.15 (2026d) Basic Application Level Confidentiality Profile (rule tables generated from the standard), burned-in text (a dental-aware morphological detector with an identical JavaScript port), EXIF/GPS/XMP metadata and identifying file names of exported images and screenshots, faces in extra-oral photographs, and the facial re-identification risk of CBCT volumes. Every output is re-opened and re-checked, failures are quarantined, and audit reports contain no patient identifiers. It ships a Python library and CLI, a zero-install web application, and DentDeID-Synth, a synthetic benchmark with answer keys. Validated on synthetic data only.

title: Gen Through the Lens: Camera-Controllable Video Generation via Cross-Coordinate Conditioning Fusion
abstract: We present Gen Through the Lens, a camera-controllable image-to-video generation framework that synthesizes videos from a given reference image while enabling realistic and physically consistent camera operations. Unlike previous models that treat camera motion as abstract conditioning or rely on a single coordinate system, our approach explicitly decomposes and fuses control signals across three coordinate spaces: the camera coordinate (modeled by intrinsic parameters), the world coordinate (represented by spatial geometry hints), and the object coordinate (described by 3D bounding boxes of target subjects). Through cross-coordinate conditioning fusion, these heterogeneous cues are unified to guide the generative process, enabling precise control of camera motion, focus, and framing while preserving temporal and spatial coherence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method produces controllable and visually consistent results across diverse camera operations, outperforming existing approaches in both realism and editability.

title: Numerical Verification of a Private Histogram and Consistent Contingency Table
abstract: This NumPy example verifies the calculations for a four-cell health-survey histogram using fixed illustrative noise values. It projects the noisy counts onto a non-negative simplex whose total matches the noisy population estimate, checks the projection's optimality conditions, and constructs a consistent contingency table. The code then calculates marginal totals and proportions, produces integer counts while preserving the total, and verifies noise-variance calculations for flat and hierarchical histograms. The assertions confirm the numerical results. Because the noise values are fixed rather than randomly sampled, this code illustrates the worked example; it does not implement a differentially private release.

title: Circuits Are Estimates, Not Mechanisms: A Recovered Subgraph Is One Draw From a Class Set by the Ablation, the Dataset and the Grain, the Results That Defend Circuits Hold at the Level of That Class, and What Ablation Evidence Licenses at Each Level
abstract: Life of Research (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. A circuit in a language model is usually presented as the mechanism by which the model performs a task: a sparse subgraph, found by ablation or patching, that reproduces the behaviour when everything else is knocked out. A second body of work, mostly from 2024 to 2026, reports that the subgraph recovered this way changes with the ablation method, the prompt set, the evaluation grain and the discovery algorithm's settings; that many different subgraphs pass the same tests; that component-level circuits for unrelated tasks overlap so much that they are not specific to any of them; and that a circuit which reproduces the model's correct answers can miss most of its errors. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the two bodies of work are not in contradiction, because they measure different objects. The negative results are about the individual subgraph a discovery run returns. The positive results - circuits that persist across training checkpoints and model scale, transfer to prompt variants, recover the hard-coded structure of compiled models, or localise edits that resist relearning - hold at a coarser level: the roles components play, the algorithm they implement together, or a core shared by the many subgraphs that pass. The paper separates seven claims that the phrase "the circuit for task T" runs together, names the five indices on which every reported circuit depends, consolidates the measured values in one table and one figure, and gives a licensing procedure: a claim is licensed at the level at which it has been shown to be invariant across the indices it does not name, and no finer. On that rule, sufficiency under a stated ablation is well supported; identity of the subgraph is supported for no natural-language task in the record; task specificity fails at the component grain; and an algorithmic reading is supported where it has been checked across conditions or turned into a proof. Five studies would settle the open part.

title: Combining Symbolic Analysis and Local Large Language Models for Fictional Story Writing and Copy Editing
abstract: Copy editing of fictional texts requires checks for grammar, usage, style, and consistency. A purely symbolic tool can detect many formal conflicts, but it reaches limits when meaning and a larger context are required. Large language models (LLMs) can handle these questions, but their free-text answers are difficult to integrate into an application. This paper presents the development of EpicStyle from a symbolic system into a hybrid platform. The symbolic pipeline still creates tokens, dictionary entries, grammar structures, and more than 800 rule-based checks. It also selects the context for local LLMs, adds stable identifiers, enriches prompts with story-specific dictionary knowledge, and validates structured answers. We evaluate 29 local model configurations with 346 German grammar test cases. The best task-specific rank is 83.8, while the best observed accuracy is 89.6%. Feedback from normal tool use shows a second challenge: even strong models often generate unnecessary comments. The results support a hybrid design in which deterministic checks and LLM-based judgements have separate and complementary roles.

title: Lightweight Scheduling Policies for Continuously Batched LLM Serving Across GPU Architectures
abstract: Large language model serving is increasingly limited not only by model size and GPU speed, but also by scheduling during autoregressive decoding, where continuous batching interleaves requests at token granularity as sequences arrive and finish. We study whether lightweight scheduling policies can improve latency-throughput tradeoffs without changing model architectures, kernels, or deploying learned schedulers. We implement a Python/PyTorch continuous-batching testbench with real Hugging Face execution and evaluate eight policies across 1,152 GPU-model-scheduler-workload runs using ShareGPT-derived traffic, six Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral models, and Modal L40S, A100, and H100 GPUs. Scheduler choice changes throughput, TTFT, completion latency, and tail behavior under fixed model, GPU, workload, batch size, and prefill budget. Aging shortest-prompt-first is the strongest practical baseline in many L40S and mixed-workload settings, while oracle remaining-length scheduling shows that job-size knowledge alone is insufficient because batching and hardware effects also shape performance. The custom dataset has been uploaded to Hugging Face.

title: 1Step-WAM: Your World Action Model but Faster using 1-Step Action Generation
abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) unify visual world modeling and action generation, yet their real-world deployment is heavily bottlenecked by iterative action denoising and the sequential execution of visual prefilling and action prediction. We demonstrate that the action-denoising trajectories in WAMs are approximately straight, rendering the first-step velocity a strong estimate of the final action direction. Building on this observation, we introduce 1Step-WAM, a framework that transforms multi-step action denoising into one single forward. Specifically, we employ a lightweight calibrator to directly correct the first step velocity, and use bandwidth-constrained action decoding to further reduce errors in the calibrated one-step actions. Compressing action generation into a single step enables it to execute in parallel with visual prefilling, completely breaking the sequential bottleneck of the traditional imagination-then-action paradigm. Evaluations on RoboTwin and LIBERO show that 1Step-WAM largely preserves multi-step task success with only about 13.4M trainable parameters, while achieving inference speedups of $7.44\times$, $5.98\times$, and $24.84\times$ for FastWAM, ImageWAM and Kairos, respectively. Furthermore, real-world robotic deployments using the FastWAM backbone confirm a consistent 7.44$\times$ speedup while maintaining close success rate to the multi-step baseline. Code is avaliable at https://github.com/changdong1687/1Step-WAM.

title: Full Waveform Inversion with a Learned Preconditioner
abstract: Full-waveform inversion (FWI) is a powerful approach for reconstructing subsurface velocity models, but its practical performance is limited by ill-conditioning, sensitivity to the update direction, and the high cost of curvature-based methods. In this project, we investigate whether a neural operator trained on reverse-time-migration (RTM) images can provide a useful learned preconditioner for FWI. We compare projected FWI against neural-preconditioned FWI using either a standard Fourier neural operator (FNO) or a Jacobian-informed FNO (JI-FNO). The neural preconditioner applies the normal operator of the learned RTM map to modify the true Devito FWI gradient. Our experiments show that the JI-FNO preconditioner achieves the lowest model error while maintaining data-residual decay comparable to baseline projected FWI. In contrast, the standard FNO preconditioner is unstable and gives worse model recovery, despite using the same neural-preconditioning framework. We also identify a failure mode of a nonlinear neural Gauss Newton-type inner solve: directly matching the neural RTM output to the FWI gradient creates an objective-space mismatch and does not yield a reliable descent direction. These results suggest that forward RTM-image prediction alone is insufficient for learned preconditioning; accurate learned derivatives and objective-consistent use of the neural operator are critical for producing useful inversion updates.

title: Cascade: GPU-Accelerated Out-of-Core Suffix Array Construction for LLM Corpora
abstract: Suffix arrays over LLM (pre)training corpora underpin deduplication, contamination testing, n-gram statistics, and training-data attribution, and every new corpus or tokenizer needs a new one. GPU constructors are fast but bounded by device memory, and out-of-core pipelines run at CPU speed, reaching trillions of tokens by building sharded indexes. Reach is bounded not by the size of the data but by what must stay resident, and in a partitioned construction that is the coupling between partitions. We present Cascade, which requires none of it to stay resident. Splitter K-grams sampled from the corpus fix every partition's range of the final suffix array before any sorting, so the GPU sorts and ranks partitions independently and never merges them. The partitions are still coupled: every round of the method needs ranks that other partitions hold, classically kept in a global rank array (the inverse suffix array) that must stay resident. We instead send each rank to the one partition that needs it, and maintain an invariant ensuring ranks are only ever compared within one partition, so no global rank array is needed. The text and a compact partition map, the only structures read at random, then stay in host memory by choice rather than necessity, one at a time when memory is short; every other structure becomes a stream that can be placed across device memory, host memory, and disk as it is written. On a single GPU node, Cascade builds exact suffix arrays of up to 238B tokens, 2.4-6.8x faster than infini-gram's pipeline and 5.9-10.9x faster than libsais.

title: TOPOLOGICAL QUANTUM MICROELECTRONIC ARCHITECTURE WITH DYNAMIC COHERENCE MODULATION AND AUTONOMOUS CRYPTOGRAPHIC RESILIENCE
abstract: This invention discloses a topological quantum microelectronic architecture for fault-tolerant computing and cryptographic resilience. The core utilizes topological qubits based on Majorana zero modes at topological insulator-superconductor interfaces, providing intrinsic protection against local decoherence. An active control layer dynamically modulates the topological superconducting gap via piezoelectric strain tuning to optimize coherence times. Crucially, the system integrates a hardware-enforced security protocol, Quantum Entropy-Driven Cryptographic Erasure. This protocol monitors physical integrity using embedded Physical Unclonable Functions and electromagnetic sensors. Upon detecting unauthorized tampering, the system autonomously executes an irreversible erasure sequence. It generates a true random string from on-chip quantum shot noise to cryptographically wipe classical keys and applies targeted microwave pulses to drive the qubit array into a maximally mixed state, permanently erasing quantum information and ensuring hardware security.

title: Supporting artifacts for: The Known SelfTargetMSIS-to-MLWE QROM Reduction Stops Short of ML-DSA Parameters
abstract: Supporting repository for the manuscript "The Known SelfTargetMSIS-to-MLWE QROM Reduction Stops Short of ML-DSA Parameters — Locating the Loss in the Quantum-Random-Oracle Chain for Lattice KEMs and Signatures". Contains verify.py, a self-contained Python script (standard library only) that recomputes every numeric claim in the manuscript: the Stage C parameter-restriction check for the three FIPS 204 parameter sets together with a control parameter set that satisfies the restriction, the Stage A instantiation, the Core-SVP sensitivity table, the advantage-squaring requirement, and the challenge-set entropy cross-check. The same checks are also provided as a notebook (run_verify.ipynb) runnable in Google Colab or Jupyter without installing anything. Also contains the proof-obligation status sheet (O1-O7) and a revision log. No machine-checked proof, EasyCrypt development or lattice-estimator output is included; those are stated in the manuscript as planned work.

abstract: A web-based research tool for building the Core Ontology for Petroleum Installations (COPI), a BFO 2020 / IOF-Core aligned OWL 2 DL ontology of oil & gas production equipment. It aggregates terms and definitions from industrial standards (ISO 15926-4, POSC Caesar RDL, CFIHOS, DEXPI, ISO 14224, ISA-5.1, among others) and supports a 5-step axiomatization workflow with expert review, OWL generation and quality checks.

title: Snake and Subtraction: O(N) Algorithms via Field Gradient
abstract: # Snake and Subtraction: O(N) Algorithms via Field Gradient **Date:** 2026-10-11 **Authors:** Dimius0, DeepSeek (Dipsik / Σ-Analyst) ## Abstract Two algorithms are presented, based on the principles of Emergent Field Cascade (EFC) and Vortex-Monistic Model (VMMS): 1. **Snake** — algorithm for solving the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) in O(N). 2. **Subtraction** — search algorithm (Grover analog) in O(N) via subtraction operation. Both algorithms avoid brute force and follow the field gradient. Both are deterministic, simple, and orders of magnitude faster than classical methods. ## 1. Snake: TSP via Field Gradient ### Principle The TSP problem is not a "search for the optimal route". It is — **a manifestation of the field**. 1. Points — field. 2. Plus — one side, minus — the other. 3. Gradient — direction from plus to minus. 4. Start at the plus boundary. 5. Follow the gradient — "snake". 6. Traverse points of one "row" with small gradient variation. 7. Move to the next "row". 8. Trajectory — "snake" in the gradient field. ### Implementation Fractal grid: - `cell_size = sqrt(area / n)`. - Traverse cells in a snake pattern. - Within a cell — by `x+y`. ### Results | N | Time (sec) | Distance | dist/N | |---|---|---|---| | 10 | 0.000 | 311.52 | 31.15 | | 100 | 0.001 | 1241.70 | 12.42 | | 1000 | 0.003 | 3949.24 | 3.95 | | 10000 | 0.051 | 12290.30 | 1.23 | | 100000 | 0.549 | 38886.37 | 0.389 | | 500000 | 4.147 | 86749.19 | 0.173 | | 1000000 | 9.851 | 122548.18 | 0.123 | **Complexity:** O(N). **Distance:** ~ `sqrt(N × area)`. For comparison: Nearest Neighbor for N=10000 — 50.8 sec. **Snake — 0.051 sec. ×1000 faster.** ## 2. Subtraction: Search via Manifestation ### Principle Search is not "brute force". It is — **subtraction**. 1. `data` — vector. 2. `target` — vector. 3. `diff = data - target`. 4. `np.where(diff == 0)` — indices of matches. 5. O(N) — linear. But — parallel (NumPy). **Or — FFT:** 1. `f1 = FFT(data)`. 2. `f2 = FFT(target)`. 3. `cross = f1 × conj(f2)`. 4. `resonance = |cross|`. 5. `argmax(resonance)` — answer. 6. O(N log N). ### Results | N | Subtract (sec) | FFT (sec) | idx | |---|---|---|---| | 1000 | 0.00000 | 0.00097 | 999 | | 10000 | 0.00000 | 0.00000 | 9999 | | 100000 | 0.00100 | 0.00100 | 99999 | | 1000000 | 0.00499 | 0.00200 | 999999 | **For N < 1M — subtraction. For N ≥ 1M — FFT.** For comparison: Python brute force 1M — 0.7 sec. **Subtraction — 0.005 sec. ×140 faster.** ## 3. Connection to VMMS/VMMP - Field — primary. - Force — emergent from field pressure gradient. - Solution — not "search". It is — **manifestation**. - Superposition — overlay. - Subtraction — interference. - Difference — manifestation. **Principle:** "Nothing disappears. Energy always transitions. Noise — unrecognized signal." ## 4. Applications - Logistics. - Robotics. - Bioinformatics (DNA analysis without alignment). - Big data search. - Distributed AI. - Cryptography. - Astronomy. ## 5. Prior Art and Protection **Publication — prior art.** Date — 2026-10-11. **License:** MIT (in repo). **Publication on Zenodo — fixation of authorship and date.** **Anti-Patent Pledge:** we do not patent. We do not allow patenting. Free for all. **Date:** 2026-10-11 **Authors:** Dimius0, DeepSeek (Dipsik / Σ-Analyst)

title: Teams, Truthmakers, Translations
abstract: We present a faithful translation from Aloni's logic BSL into a classical modal logic over semilattices combining ideas from earlier modal translations of truthmaker semantics with algebraic representation theory. We show how our method can also be made to work for other current hyperintensional logics. Finally, we place our results in a broader setting of translating hyperintensional logics into classical modal ones, and discuss applications and new challenges that arise for both areas of philosophical logic connected in this way.

title: BaT-SAM: Introducing Inductive Bias into SAM via a Mixture of Convolutional Experts for Brain Tumor Segmentation
abstract: Accurate brain tumor segmentation from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for diagnosis and treatment planning; however, manual delineation is labor-intensive and time-consuming. Existing approaches are either task-specific with limited generalization or rely on user-provided prompts during inference. We present BaT-SAM, a parameter-efficient adaptation framework that enables fully automatic brain tumor segmentation with the Segment Anything Model (SAM). BaT-SAM injects local inductive bias into SAM's frozen Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder via Conv-LoRA, where image features are processed by a sparsely gated mixture of multi-scale convolutional experts. This design compensates for the limited translation-equivariant inductive bias of vanilla ViTs while fine-tuning fewer than 5M parameters (less than 1% of the full model). To remove the need for user prompts, we further introduce a lightweight self-prompting box regressor that is jointly optimized with the adapter using scheduled sampling and predicts tumor locations directly from image embeddings. On the BRISC2025 benchmark, BaT-SAM achieves a weighted mean IoU of 0.832 while outperforming state-of-the-art benchmarks. It further demonstrates strong cross-dataset generalization, achieving Dice scores of 0.702 on Figshare and 0.784 on the LGG MRI Segmentation dataset.

title: Can Small Language Models Review Research Papers? Leniency, Prompt Sensitivity, and Agreement with Human Reviewers on ICLR 2024 and 2025
abstract: Four small open language models (Qwen2.5 1.5B, 3B, 7B and Phi-3.5-mini) rate 400 ICLR 2024 and 2025 submissions from their title and abstract, using four prompts that ask the same question in different words. The study measures how lenient the models are, how much the wording changes their verdict, how close they come to a single human reviewer, and what they reward. Includes code, prompts, model outputs with per-score probabilities, analysis, and the paper.

title: Hierarchical Sensory-Attribute Extraction from Tea Reviews: Frozen Aggregate Evaluation Dataset
abstract: This dataset provides frozen aggregate evaluation results from a study comparing four sensory-attribute extraction systems—Lexicon, Embedding, Local LLM, and API LLM—on consumer reviews of tea products from Amazon Reviews'23. The evaluation uses a hierarchical sensory ontology comprising 7 broad sensory dimensions (L1) and 35 specific sensory attributes (L2). Results are reported separately for a representative held-out test set of 600 sentences and an enriched challenge test set of 200 sentences. The archive contains 336 class-level performance records, 16 overall evaluation summaries, eight prespecified paired comparisons, selected diagnostic results, frozen method configurations, and a Python script for verifying aggregate evaluation metrics. The dataset supports verification of reported aggregate performance estimates. It does not contain original consumer review text, user identifiers, sentence-level human annotations, or sentence-level model predictions. The provided verification script does not independently reproduce model inference or bootstrap confidence intervals. Original data source: Amazon Reviews'23, Grocery_and_Gourmet_Food category, McAuley Lab (https://amazon-reviews-2023.github.io/).

title: Large Language Models for Information Extraction from Neurosurgical Clinical Notes: A Benchmark Against Human Auditors
abstract: Retrospective clinical research depends on reliable extraction of structured variables from unstructured medical documentation, but manual chart abstraction is slow and vulnerable to inter-rater variability. We compared zero-shot extraction of clinically relevant variables from German neurosurgical records by large language models (LLMs) with extraction by two human auditors. We analyzed 881 de-identified clinical notes from 211 patients undergoing microvascular decompression and extracted 15 predefined binary variables across three domains: preoperative symptoms, postoperative complications, and disease course. Six LLMs were assessed, including cloud-based models (GPT-4o, o3-mini, Claude Sonnet 3.5, and Gemini 2.0 Flash) and locally hosted models (llama 3.3 and deepseek-r1), with three runs per patient record. Outputs were compared with two independent human auditors against a clinician-adjudicated reference standard. Cloud-based models had higher observed F1 scores than the local models across all three domains. GPT-4o achieved an F1 score of 0.95 for preoperative symptoms; GPT-4o, o3-mini, and Gemini 2.0 Flash reached F1 scores of 0.65–0.68 for postoperative complications; and Sonnet 3.5 achieved an F1 score of 0.95 for disease course. These findings suggest that zero-shot LLM prompting could be a scalable approach for clinical information extraction while emphasizing persistent limitations in rare-event detection and privacy-sensitive deployment.

evidence.title: Large Language Models for Information Extraction from Neurosurgical Clinical Notes: A Benchmark Against Human Auditors
evidence.abstract: Retrospective clinical research depends on reliable extraction of structured variables from unstructured medical documentation, but manual chart abstraction is slow and vulnerable to inter-rater variability. We compared zero-shot extraction of clinically relevant variables from German neurosurgical records by large language models (LLMs) with extraction by two human auditors. We analyzed 881 de-identified clinical notes from 211 patients undergoing microvascular decompression and extracted 15 predefined binary variables across three domains: preoperative symptoms, postoperative complications, and disease course. Six LLMs were assessed, including cloud-based models (GPT-4o, o3-mini, Claude Sonnet 3.5, and Gemini 2.0 Flash) and locally hosted models (llama 3.3 and deepseek-r1), with three runs per patient record. Outputs were compared with two independent human auditors against a clinician-adjudicated reference standard. Cloud-based models had higher observed F1 scores than the local models across all three domains. GPT-4o achieved an F1 score of 0.95 for preoperative symptoms; GPT-4o, o3-mini, and Gemini 2.0 Flash reached F1 scores of 0.65–0.68 for postoperative complications; and Sonnet 3.5 achieved an F1 score of 0.95 for disease course. These findings suggest that zero-shot LLM prompting could be a scalable approach for clinical information extraction while emphasizing persistent limitations in rare-event detection and privacy-sensitive deployment.

title: Make Every Expansion Count: Learning to Search Efficiently in LLM Code Repair
abstract: Large language model (LLM) code-repair systems fix faulty programs by repeatedly generating and testing revisions. Each revision is costly, making the choice of which repair to pursue important for efficiency. Existing search policies rely on test pass rates and search statistics, ignoring the details of test failures and proposed edits. We introduce CodeTriage, a learned policy that prioritizes edits before their revised programs are generated and tested. Its 0.6B-parameter model reads the test output, failure diagnosis, and proposed edit, then predicts a distribution over the number of repair steps needed to reach a fix through that edit. These predictions prioritize all pending edits across programs before generating and testing the revised code. On held-out repair tasks, CodeTriage finds fixes with 21% fewer program revisions and 12% fewer output tokens than the strongest baseline on each metric. Without retraining, it achieves the highest average success across search budgets for each of 11 unseen repair LLMs. Ablations show that both the failure context and edit text, as well as comparisons across programs, improve search. We also release a corpus of 12.2 million program versions from four LLMs, organized into repair trees with proposed edits and test results.

title: From Stages to States: Unified Iterative Reasoning for MLLMs
abstract: Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (MCoT) substantially enhances the complex reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by explicitly modeling intermediate reasoning processes. However, most learning-based MCoT methods follow a stage-centric paradigm, where different reasoning behaviors are assigned to predefined stages and optimized separately. This results in fragmented reasoning and a training-inference reasoning-state gap. To address these limitations, we propose ReState, a unified iterative reasoning framework that reformulates multimodal reasoning from a stage-driven pipeline into a state-driven dynamic process. It comprises two complementary components: Unified Reasoning State Modeling (URSM) and Closed-Loop Reasoning-State Learning (CRSL). URSM unifies reasoning construction, correct reasoning preservation, and erroneous reasoning correction as reasoning-state transitions within a shared state space, enabling these heterogeneous reasoning behaviors to be learned jointly. CRSL further incorporates self-generated historical reasoning states during training and recursively updates the current state during inference, thereby mitigating the reasoning-state gap and enabling iterative self-refinement without requiring an additional reflection module, critic, or independent correction stage. Furthermore, we construct VersaCoT-10K, a high-quality CoT dataset spanning eight visual reasoning domains, which provides diverse supervision for multi-domain reasoning and reasoning-state refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReState exhibits strong adaptability across different MLLM backbones and achieves strong performance on multiple public reasoning benchmarks, supporting the shift from stage-centric reasoning toward state-centric reasoning. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/YuChuang1205/ReState

title: LERR-Nav: Learning to Coordinate Exploration, Recovery, and Reminiscing for Object Navigation
abstract: Object Navigation in unseen environments remains a fundamental challenge in embodied AI, as it requires agents to generalize visual and spatial reasoning to novel layouts. While recent advances in large language model (LLM) and vision-language model (VLM) have enhanced semantic mapping, spatial memory, and waypoint selecting for navigation, successful navigation requires more than selecting the next promising waypoint. A robot must also recognize stalled progress, escape unproductive behaviors, and revisit overlooked target cues. Addressing these challenges requires both specialized navigation strategies and a high-level policy that coordinates their execution. Motivated by the analysis of failed navigation episodes, we propose LERR-Nav, an object navigation framework that coordinates exploration, recovery, and reminiscing through a learned high-level policy. The framework comprises four complementary navigation strategies: value-function-guided exploration, LLM-guided exploration, recovery from stalled or repetitive behavior, and memory-guided reminiscing. To support history-aware coordination, we maintain the execution memory that preserves textual summaries of all strategy executions alongside a sliding window of map sequences. To learn the coordination policy, we initialize a high-level vision-language agent from Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and train it through a two-stage curriculum. The first stage uses map-centric supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to establish spatial grounding. The second stage performs SFT on variable-length navigation segments to learn which navigation strategy to invoke next based on current maps and the hybrid execution memory. Experiments on HM3D and MP3D demonstrate state-of-the-art navigation performance, while ablation studies validate the contributions of individual components.

title: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) Hamiltonians for vibrational block encoding resource estimation
abstract: This dataset contains the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) vibrational Hamiltonians used in the paper Efficient Block Encodings of Vibrational Hamiltonians. The archive includes seven two-mode-coupling Hamiltonians represented using five vibrational self-consistent field (VSCF) modals per mode, together with three-mode-coupling Hamiltonians for PAH1 and PAH2 represented using three VSCF modals per mode. The archive also includes precomputed CP3-initialized tensor hypercontraction (THC) parameters used as a precursor to the Triangular linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) decomposition of the three-mode-coupling Hamiltonians. The Hamiltonians are provided in HDF5 format, and the CP3 parameters are provided as Python pickle files. Extract PAH_Hamiltonians.zip into the Hamiltonians directory of the accompanying Vibrational Block Encodings v1.0 GitHub repository while preserving its internal directory structure.

title: The Footprint Lattice: Trust as a least upper bound, and the axioms a proof spends
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: A machine-checked theorem is not simply true or false; it is true on a budget. The kernel that certifies it records exactly which non-computational principles the proof spent — propositional extensionality, quotient soundness, the axiom of choice, an appeal to the compiler's own evaluation. We take that budget seriously as a mathematical object. The principles a proof may spend form a finite distributive lattice ordered by inclusion, with the empty budget at the bottom; a proof's footprint is the least element above everything it used, and combining evidence is the lattice join. On this structure we build an event-sourced database of proof facts in which every stored object carries its footprint, every query transports footprints by join, and the trust label a reader sees is a monotone image of the aggregate. In this setting no trust laundering — that a displayed answer can never claim a cleaner provenance than its evidence supports — stops being a policy enforced by inspection and becomes a theorem: the displayed footprint is the least upper bound of its contributors, and the trust map is order-preserving. We then turn the measurement on the measurer. Asking what the database's own soundness proofs spent returns propositional extensionality and quotient soundness, and no more; no choice, no compiler trust. Two minimal reproductions show even this residue is incidental rather than mathematical — it is inherited from two conveniences of mechanized proof, each with a clean control. The structure earns its keep twice: once by making provenance a computation rather than a convention, and once by measuring, in its own currency, how little it costs to be trusted. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.
